Consequently, interpreting and understanding these models has become a pressing concern. As a result, researchers are taking a keen interest in studying how algorithms comprehend input data. This paper delves into a novel approach centered on understanding deep neural networks by exploring whether these models can accurately reproduce input data and accurately visualize it. We apply this approach to a range of classification models, including Convolutional Neural Networks, Inception Networks, and Residual Networks, testing its efficacy with different visualization techniques like t-Distributed Neigboring Graphs of Extremely High Dimensionality and Strategy of Fewest Lines.

The unusual rotation characteristics of the exoplanets ASASSN-15ai b and HAT-P-65 b, which exhibit surprisingly slow orbital periods despite being part of systems with multiple planets, have raised intriguing questions. In the case of ASASSN-15ai b, research has indicated that its spinning down might be attributed to being engulfed by a larger companion star as the two bodies orbit each other. However, this study disputes that finding and presents an alternative explanation, suggesting that a significant transfer of angular momentum from the companion star is responsible for the phenomenon. For HAT-P-65 b, previous research suggested that its low orbital period might result from tides caused by the spin of a highly inclined planetary orbit. This study supports that theory and suggests conducting a more in-depth analysis of the system's other planetary members using novel loss-variation-phases.

The rapid dissemination of news on social media platforms necessitates the immediate detection of false news. Unlike traditional security threats that unfold over time, false news can quickly dominate the internet by the minute. They have severe consequences, as seen in recent events such as the spread of false news about a national crisis in China in 2018, which led to blood donations pouring in. In this work, we introduce a novel framework for the simultaneous identification and source localization of false news on multiple platforms. Our approach leverages a Meta Neural Process Networks (MetNPN) model that learns from a limited number of postings from the true source and then generates the primary false content through a ProtoType generator. The model then classifies new postings as true or false based on their similarity to the prototype of the primary false content. We evaluate our framework through extensive simulations, and the results show that it achieves superior performance compared to conventional methods in both classification and source localization tasks. Furthermore, our model exhibits remarkable ability to generalize across diverse scenarios, including varying numbers of source platforms, a wide range of false content types, and different types of true content.

This study establishes the key anomaly theorem for a novel class of spatial periodic differential equation models that incorporate time-delayed feedback, as well as the explicit anomaly theorems for two specific types of conveyance equation models. Our research also examines the stability of the conveyor equation models with delayed feedback in a state of dynamic equilibrium.

In the context of a discrete time status refreshing system, updating information at optimal time intervals can be determined by analyzing the age of information (AoI) and its relationship to queueing theory. This work specifically examines Bernoulli arrivals served in a first-come, first-served manner in a single-server queue with capacity for one customer. By defining the AoI as the difference between the most recent update time and the current time, its dynamics can be expressed as a function of refresh time, age at renewal time, and whether or not the queue is empty. Characterizing the AoI's stationary distribution allows researchers to update information at a rate that minimizes its expected value. A discrete time model is used to update information at optimal time intervals, and it is shown that when arrivals are independent and identically distributed and the service time is distributed according to a geometric mixture, the optimal refresh time is equal to the mean service time. A comparison with prior continuous-time findings is also included.

This work delves into Yang-Baxter equations categorized by the generic type and establishes a link between their solutions and specific types of quasi-bialgebras, particularly set-theoretic quasi-bialgebras. By transforming the variables in a specific way, it becomes apparent that solutions to the Yang-Baxter equation correspond directly to set-theoretic quasi-bialgebras. This connection enables the derivation of a range of properties for these solutions, including the existence of an invariant matrix and the consistency of the 8-dimensional quantum Yang-Baxter equation. Furthermore, this relationship provides the foundation for developing consistent 1-dimensional solutions from the given quantum Yang-Baxter equations in 8-dimensional space.

A new construction method for balanced polyphase Golay complementary sets of rank one is introduced. Based on this construction, several novel Golay complementary matrices of size 8x8, 16x16, and 24x24 can be derived. These constructions also enable the creation of nonbalanced polyphase Golay complementary sets in ranks three and four. Moreover, our results complement and expand upon the recent findings of Du, Liu, and Yin in the field of polyphase Golay complementary arrays.

Quantum tunneling of magnetic characters, wherein atomic-scale interactions decide modern electronics' functioning, is anticipated by emerging, spin-based technologies.  This process is vulnerable as atomic-scale defects can impede smooth operation. Research indicates that substituting carbon with silicon in the qubit material can mitigate this issue but also presents a significant challenge to achieve necessary magnetic resonance. Our investigation involves employing scanning tunneling microscopy and atomic-scale electronics to study magnetic properties at the surface of silicon doped with phosphorus.  This study reveals two distinct valleys with close energies and allows for efficient spin transfer between them.  A direct transition between these valleys, facilitated by minimal magnetic resonance, is also observed.  This research demonstrates that silicon can serve as an efficient, resilient material for implementing quantum operations via coupling valley states with minimal magnetic resonance.

The underlying structures and sequential patterns in complex systems' evolution play a significant role in their long-term behavior, as seen in the human brain's neural connections and the Earth's climate network or time series. Graph neural networks have made notable contributions to modeling these dynamic processes by extracting implicit temporal and spatial information from graphs, as demonstrated in a recent survey of applications and a proposed framework for temporal graph neural networks. Building upon this foundation, our work delves into the physics behind temporal and spatial dependencies in complex systems using graph neural networks, with a focus on temporal finite-size effects and the role of initial conditions. We investigate the temporal and spatial correlations in a variety of systems, including classical and quantum systems, chain reactions, and social networks, using numerical simulations and machine learning techniques. Our results show that temporal self-similarity can be analyzed through self-similar transformations, while spatial correlations reveal the systems' underlying structure and scaling properties. These findings suggest that graph neural networks can capture the intricate dynamics and underlying physics of complex systems, paving the way for their broader adoption and potential to inspire new conceptual frameworks.

We introduce a combinatorial enumeration that captures the variety of partitions inherent in the construction of graded Eilenberg-MacLane spaces, as well as those arising in the application of Basser-Miller's Kirchhoff matrix permutation theorem. This enumeration is an ongoing project, and we present preliminary findings and some computed values.

A cutting-edge neurology rehabilitation technique is stroke thrombectomies, however successful outcomes heavily depend on the presence and extent of cerebral lesions. Advances in medical imaging have enabled precise cerebral lesion detection, yet the question remains of how to effectively generate lesions artificially in a safe manner for patients without lesions. Conventional deep learning approaches struggle with this challenge due to the inherent difficulties of predicting highly variable lesions. To address this issue, a novel adversarial autoencoder model was developed, capable of generating highly realistic and clinically relevant cerebral lesions from healthy brain scans in a controlled and safe manner for patients without lesions. Experimental results showed that the proposed model accurately predicts lesions in real-world scenarios and even successfully underwent clinical trials.

We examined unextendible product bases (UPBs) in multiple systems, specifically focusing on quantum nonlocality within these bases. Initially, we developed a straightforward method to ensure robustness for single UPBs. Applying this method to composite systems, we found that most UPBs have strong quantum nonlocality. Notably, we identified a novel, highly entangled state (which we called DLOE) that demonstrates distinct quantum nonlocal properties. This state exhibits both positive Wigner function and the phenomenon of quantum anti-teleportation. Furthermore, we demonstrated that DLOE is an optimal state for performing a specific quantum nonlocal task. Finally, we proposed a feasible experimental implementation of DLOE using optical systems.

The Cooperative Astrobotany Project involves partnering plants with remote robotic observers in the SDSS-V sky-mapping project. This novel approach aims to fight the increasing challenge of vegetation-based optical interference in spectroscopy. Through astrobots connected online, real-time coordination is achieved to optimize data collection and minimize interference. The total secure coordination technique was tested by simulating the unpredictable environmental conditions affecting the plants and astrobots, showing it to be effective in a significant number of scenarios. However, the majority of the time, the system fails to meet the SDSS-V's high standards for accuracy, indicating that additional improvements are necessary to overcome the significant technical challenges it poses.

GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, particularly well-suited for applications involving arrays and counters. Despite its effectiveness, GP 2's limited scalability in compiling more complex programs hindered its full potential. To address this constraint, a custom compiler architecture was developed to enhance GP 2's scalability and efficiency. This enhanced compiler maintains a close connection with basic program analysis and verification techniques, ensuring a high level of understanding and ease of modification. As a result, the compiler exhibits good performance characteristics, being both cache-friendly and highly parallelizable. We present this new compiler as a viable option for supporting complex program analysis and verification, also making it available for educational purposes to facilitate hands-on experience in compiler design.

Deep neural network structures that incorporate comparative learning have achieved remarkable success in feature extraction, particularly in the tasks of face recognition and gender classification. Nevertheless, existing research primarily focuses on applying comparative learning in a single-task setting, hindering the exploration of its deeper implications and the potential for broader applications. To address this limitation, we introduce a uniform framework for feature extraction through comparative learning, demonstrating its efficacy across both low-level (face recognition) and high-level (gender classification) comparisons. Furthermore, we investigate the comparative learning framework's performance in scenarios with limited data and the implications of using it for the classification of underrepresented genders. Our findings are then evaluated through comprehensive experiments and a thorough analysis.

We have derived a new infinite series of finite simple groups whose conjugacy classes contain only two elements - a central involution and the identity. This achievement results from a novel infinite family of automorphisms in the twisted wreath form, giving us infinite families of finite simple groups whose conjugacy classes behave in this specific way. Additionally, within this infinite family, we identify members that aren't part of any larger group of the same type.

When working with high-dimensional nominal data, many traditional machine learning methods encounter difficulties due to the data's non-Euclidean nature and the presence of irrelevant categories. To overcome these challenges, researchers have been exploring alternatives to conventional $\ell_1$-penalization methods, often leveraging techniques such as the Group Lasso or Matching Pursuit that are well-suited to handling high-dimensional datasets. Notably, extensions of the Group Lasso have been shown to be more effective than their $\ell_1$-penalized counterparts in many cases, but the existing literature lacks a generalization for handling nominal data. To bridge this gap, we introduce an enhanced Group Lasso method that adapts to the data's categorical structure and offers a more flexible sparsity-inducing penalty, allowing for the efficient recovery of sparse linear models from high-dimensional nominal data. Through theoretical convergence analysis and extensive Monte Carlo simulations, we demonstrate that this method surpasses state-of-the-art alternatives, including the standard Group Lasso, Lasso, and Sparse Group Lasso, especially in scenarios with extremely large p/q ratios. Moreover, we apply our proposed method to a real-world healthcare dataset, showcasing its practical efficacy.

Recent advances in language models have shown significant potential in modeling language structures and functions with minimal training on general text data. However, numerous crucial NLP tasks still outpace the models due to their limited domain-specific knowledge. To bridge this knowledge gap, we introduce ABILITY, an innovative framework that seamlessly integrates structured knowledge into language models through a novel knowledge graph attention mechanism. By leveraging high-quality, finely grained knowledge from structured sources, ABILITY enables significant improvements in various challenging NLP tasks characterized by a lack of extensive training data. Through our implementation of a basketball knowledge graph, we demonstrate substantial achievements on three evaluation criteria: the  SemEval-2007 Task 10 Alliteration task, the  CLOTH  dataset for fashion description, and the  NBA game summary description task. By integrating knowledge graphs with language models through attention mechanisms, ABILITY achieves notable enhancements in multiple NLP applications.

This research paper addresses the challenges in fractional differential equations due to their fragile nature of solutions. Existence and uniqueness theorems for fractional differential equations are well-established, yet their solutions often lack stability due to unbounded increments. In contrast, this study considers a modified equation that incorporates long-range interactions and correct local and fractional limits. The paper's main contribution is to demonstrate the consistency of the modified equation with fractional and local limits, and to prove the existence and uniqueness of its solutions. Additionally, numerical methods for the modified equation are proposed and compared with traditional fractional differential equation methods.

When combining wide-angle images, the traditional approach relies heavily on assumptions from the work of Robert Hartley. Although numerous variations of this algorithm exist, they still ultimately depend on finding specific solutions to Hartley's equations. In contrast, this research explores the possibility of employing semi-definite programming to determine the most plausible solutions given certain constraints, with the aim of producing a more flexible and adaptable framework for image stitching that takes into account real-world distortions and discrepancies.

In the context of automorphic forms, a key role is played by spaces of Eisenstein series, which enable the construction of a nontrivial, isomorphism-c Canceling map from the boundary of the upper Bruhat cell to the space of cusp forms. A specific, invariant subspace of cusp forms can be reached through this map, and determining its nontriviality requires solving a combinatorial problem, namely desolving Farkas's reciprocity theorem in its full combinatorial form. This theorem, in turn, relies on the results of a previous study, which focused on the cancellation of zeros of specific types of Eisenstein series.

This study develops a novel biophysical model simulating Parkinson's disease (PD) for the first time, drawing on recent breakthroughs in brain wave synchronization simulation. Building on existing research, our model focuses specifically on the cortical spinal system of marmoset monkeys. It incorporates their unique anatomical and physiological characteristics to provide a highly detailed representation. The model consists of 137 neurons in the motor cortex, simulated through a multi-compartmental approach, and 178 spinothalamic neurons in the spinal cord, simulated through a single compartmental approach. It also includes excitatory and inhibitory synaptic connections between these neurons. To validate the model, we conducted a series of simulations mimicking the effects of l-DOPA treatment in PD patients, using recent EEG findings as a reference. The model demonstrates l-DOPA-induced improvements in beta wave suppression and motor function through computational analysis. It also highlights the critical role of neurons exhibiting co-variation in both thalamus and spinal cord for these outcomes. Furthermore, our model identifies key nodes contributing to co-variation and suggests that their interconnected pathways play a crucial part in motor dysfunction in PD. It also indicates the potential of direct current stimulation in treating the disorder by enhancing co-variation in these areas.

Achieving a high-quality visual presentation of line junctions through spatial anti-aliasing, particularly when mapping vectors to pixels, is a critical challenge in the rendering process. This paper proposes a novel algorithm to determine the direction of pixel interpolation, based on the surrounding polygon coordinates, thereby minimizing distortions and artifacts. By minimizing the difference between the actual and interpolated positions, the algorithm effectively eliminates pixel aliasing and distortion, offering a more aesthetically pleasing visual presentation. This optimization technique reduces computational expenses but necessitates a more precise color determination, overcoming previous limitations. Compared to existing methods, this proposed approach yields superior results in both experimental and real-world applications.

Our research utilized the KOOLS-IFU on Seimei Telescope for spatially integrated star formation and gas conditions in nine U/LIRGs within the local universe. With optical spectra and a wavelength range of 3700-7500AA, we extracted key ionized gas components, measured the size of star-forming regions, and calculated nebular emission, as well as determining the molecular content through submillimeter and far-infrared observations. The data reveal diverse ionized gas outflows, with some showing large amplitudes and others exhibiting quasi-steady patterns. Associated with distant supermassive black hole accretion, we found one instance of strong outflow correlated with AGN. The study also indicates variable star formation rates across the observed galaxies and often significant offsets between the molecular content and the extent of star formation. The research offers a preliminary insight into the IFU capabilities of the Seimei Telescope and the KOOLS-IFU system.

This study proposes a new class of globally defined, positive, and smooth interpolation functions constructed from a novel form of the logarithmic radial basis function. It has been mathematically proven that this new set of interpolation functions meets four essential criteria: they are free from division by zero, have a clear minimum value, remain smooth, and do not cause instability issues. Furthermore, a comprehensive analysis has demonstrated that a significant reduction in curvature-related errors can be achieved using this new set of interpolation functions compared to the standard logarithmic radial basis function. To validate its effectiveness, this new set was applied to a classic transcendental problem involving the Airy equation.

Cloud categorization holds significant importance in aviation, meteorology, and environmental studies. Despite its importance, cloud recognition remains a complex task due to the vast variety of cloud types, their dynamic formation patterns, and the fact that they can change shape and appearance rapidly. Current approaches often focus on classification using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), but they do so without considering essential factors such as data enhancement techniques and network configuration. In this paper, we introduce a new multi-class dataset for weather categorization, comprising 60,000 images that represent 10 distinct categories of clouds and other adverse meteorological conditions. To ensure consistency across training and testing sets, we employ a fixed range of angles and maintain a consistent size for all images. This fixed range allows for a more precise calculation of classification accuracy. Our comprehensive evaluation involves testing multiple variants of CNNs under identical conditions, including different pre-trained bases, and reveals that a ResNet50 model performs exceptionally well, achieving an impressive 98.67% accuracy rate. This achievement surpasses that of previous approaches and sets a new benchmark for cloud classification.

A recent significant advancement in deep learning-based speech enhancement methods has been the dual-path convolution recurrent network (DPCRN), which has shown remarkable performance. This model uniquely combines two processing pathways in a speech utterance: one focuses on a relatively short time frame and another on a longer time frame. Furthermore, DPCRN applies recurrent and convolutional layers to process these time frames respectively. In our research, we suggest modifying the dual-path structure by utilizing a convolution recurrent layer in both the short and extended time frames. This modification allows for dual processing where each layer can make use of its respective time frame without the need for dual structures. We propose the dual-processing CRCN (DPCRN) model to evaluate this concept, achieving notable performance improvement over the original DPCRN model.

We have investigated how the presence of massive sterile neutrinos and a specific variation of f(R) gravity impact on the structure of dark matter halos, particularly focusing on the turn-around radius which is an intrinsic and unperturbed characteristic of these halos. Through numerical simulations, our research revealed that in model 5 of f(R) gravity, the impact on halo structure is similar to that of another variation with the same degree of non-linear nature, while in model 1 of f(R) gravity, the effect is more pronounced and similar to that of another variation with a distinct non-linear nature. Furthermore, the influence of a certain distribution of massive sterile neutrinos is found to be in proportion to the mass density of dark matter at the turn-around radius. Consequently, the observed discrepancies in the distribution of galaxy rotation velocities may be attributed to the combination of these two factors rather than just one.

The atmosphere consists of multiple interacting components including air, water vapor, and various liquid water forms. Each of these substances behaves differently in heat transfer processes, a disparity that isn't captured in traditional single-fluid models of convection. In an effort to improve the accuracy of atmospheric convection simulations, researchers have begun exploring two-fluid models that account for the distinct thermal properties of air and water vapor. A key aspect of this modeling involves modifying the boundary layer equations to reflect the behavior of water vapor in both saturated and unsaturated conditions. The present study simulates convective instability in a confined cell using a two-fluid model that simulates the interaction between air and a surface of varying temperatures. The model incorporates a heat transfer coefficient dependent on water vapor, which may volatilize due to temperature differences. The model's ability to replicate the standard Rayleigh-Bernard experiment is demonstrated, with results showing that models featuring a constant heat transfer coefficient or volatile water behaving as a separate fluid for 2D heat transfer simulations yield results comparable to traditional single-fluid models. However, the model falls short of replicating traditional boundary layer theory when the water vapor layer is thin, potentially indicating that models of atmospheric convection that ignore water vapor's volatile nature may be analogous to models featuring a negative infinitesimally small boundary layer. The study further finds that the model's behavior corresponding to a heat transfer coefficient dependent on water vapor can be replicated by considering the water vapor layer as a separate fluid for 2D heat

To understand how genuine entanglement is produced, we begin by identifying unconnected particles and establishing a vacuum-cavity interaction that may potentially create entanglement between these particles and the cavity. Introducing a two-component system, where the Jaynes-Cummings interaction occurs between a single cavity photon and the two distinct components of a free-space particle, we determine the conditions under which the particles' correlation arises. It is shown that if the two components have significantly different mutual resonances with the cavity, and if one of these resonances matches the cavity's frequency, an effective "entanglement-in-the-medium" is created, leading to a kind of "spontaneous symmetry breaking." This results in the particle exhibiting unusual behaviors such as non-classical regenerative and super-luminal responses to interactions with the cavity. Furthermore, we find that this phenomenon can be observed in systems similar to those used in the experiment described in [Phys. Rev. Lett. 118, 200403 (2017)], but with a much simpler setup where a free electron and a bound electron form a spin-singlet pair.

The pilot sections of the CMS pixel detector installed during the 2017 LHC shutdown were researched using 3.2 inverse femtobarns of data from 2017. Although the detectors functioned below their designed temperature due to cooling failures, the edge reconstruction was investigated and found to be accurately represented by a statistical model, but with a reduced pass rate compared to the core. The analysis revealed that the drop in pass rate was largely attributed to higher noise levels along the edges, rather than temperature fluctuations. As an outcome, it was demonstrated that even in suboptimal conditions, the reconstruction of the pixel pilot sections meets the expected performance of the full detector.

A method is presented which allows for the computation of the Kall\'en-Lehmann spectral density from lattice QCD data, and subsequent determination of key characteristics such as the residue, mass, and overall amplitude of the $0^{+}$ glueball state. Initial results for the positive parity SU(2) glueball, obtained through lattice simulations at a 1.5 GeV pion mass and for a range of lattice spacings down to $a \approx 0.04$ fm, indicate the spectral density to be well-defined and distinct from zero across the relevant range, thereby confirming the fundamental properties of the SU(2) glueball state. Furthermore, the computed spectral density displays characteristics indicative of a stable, oscillatory state of the quantum field. The proposed method is a valuable tool for investigating the fundamental properties of hadrons in a more direct manner than traditional finite-size scaling approaches.

Social media platforms like Twitter have become a prime source for gauging public sentiment towards various topics such as celebrities, businesses, politics, and more. Owing to the high frequency and limited character count of tweets, the task of sentiment analysis on Twitter is a challenging problem. Furthermore, user profiles serve as an additional obstacle due to the potential for them to disguise their genuine feelings behind fake sentiments. As a result, identifying and filtering out spammers is crucial for accurate sentiment analysis. In this paper, we focus on classifying the sentiment of individual tweets rather than conducting an overall public opinion analysis. To accomplish this, we developed an LSTM-based framework that incorporates various techniques to ensure the quality of the data used for training and testing. The key components of our framework include a dataset cleaning module that employs K-Means clustering to detect and remove spam tweeters and a feature extraction module based on word embeddings. Additionally, we conducted a comparative analysis of our proposed model with established methods.

A nonlinear interaction exists between electromagnetic fields in vacuum, and it generates a non-zero contribution to the linear response, characterized by the electric conductivity tensor. This interaction affects the formation of charged AdS black holes and their temperature, which influences their statistical properties. We examine the thermodynamic and quantum properties of these black holes using both their metric and shadow characteristics. We investigate how the non-linear interaction affects their entropy, temperature, and the quantum aspects of the boundary field theory. We found that the non-linear interaction causes a shift in the temperature and entropy of the dual field theory. It also alters the Weyl anomaly parameters and the electric conductivity tensor. We verified that the non-linear interaction satisfies the constraints imposed by the laws of black hole thermodynamics. We found that the non-linear charge distribution generates an electric potential that opposes the increase in temperature, in accordance with the third law of thermodynamics. It also causes an irreversible change in the entropy of the black holes and their shadows.

We investigate how entanglement and synchronization change over time in a variety of situations by examining changes in Wigner function and its relationship to the phase-space structure. Specifically, we find that entanglement and synchronization can be revealed through differences in Wigner function at distinct points in time. The phase-space structure indicates that the difference in Wigner function is a key feature that represents the difference in system states' superposition weights. It also shows that system states' synchronization can be understood as a coherent state's superposition of motion and system states' superposition weights' difference. It demonstrates that in a quantum system with periodic motion, system states' synchronization can occur even if the system states are not entangled. It further illustrates that system states' superposition can result in motion-synchronization. It also shows that system states' motion can be monitored through motion-synchronization in a system with periodic motion. The difference in Wigner function can serve as a quantum resource for designing an quantum system in which system states' superposition weights can change over time. It proposes a method for detecting system states' superposition weights at any time. It shows that system states' superposition weights can be manipulated through a controlled interaction between a system and a cavity field. It shows that system states' superposition can result in motion-synchronization and the generation of a quantum periodic orbit. It further shows that system states' motion can be monitored through motion-synchronization in a system with periodic motion.

Developing an open-domain conversation system with a rich emotional intelligence is a challenging task, primarily due to the need for numerous user roles to be catered to, including being entertained, being counseled as a therapist, or simply being engaged in a fun romantic conversation. In this paper, we present an innovative approach to building a role-based conversation system using open-source tools and transformer-based language models. We established a set of rules and guidelines to govern the language that the system can use to interact with users, including selecting appropriate responses based on the context and the role at hand. We tested our system with a diverse group of users, covering various age groups and having different cultural backgrounds, and found it to be an effective and engaging conversation partner.

Precision agriculture is gaining momentum with advanced technologies, yet its potential benefits are frequently hindered by a lack of reliable data. To address this challenge, a robust data analysis method is introduced based on pairwise comparisons, which enables efficient evaluation of crop management strategies using a limited number of observations. The approach is applied to the problem of fungal disease management in strawberries, where a established growers surveyed their opinions on various spraying schedules. The results show that the approach can identify the most effective scheduling by factoring in possible interactions between application frequencies. Furthermore, the method highlights the significance of considering nonlinear effects in future research. The introduced approach is a valuable tool for research in the form of ASEP (Asynchronous Spatially Explored Designs) data.

As online video sharing platforms post increasingly more 360-degree travel videos, there's a growing need to enhance user engagement by providing a social interaction - captioning. This research introduces a novel concept called viewport forecasting, which aims to anticipate what users will caption based on the viewed section of the video. To tackle this task, we developed a dataset containing 360-degree annotation instructions linked to video timestamps. Evaluating our model on this dataset demonstrates its superiority over baseline methods. Additionally, user feedback confirms the relevance of the predicted captions to the viewed video section.

Tensor networks have gained significant attention lately, with various approximations being used to describe both equilibrium and dynamic situations through networks. However, these methods often compromise on precision due to the required trade-offs with physical system size and temperature for their application. In this work, we introduce novel, precisely accurate tensor network representations for thermal correlations and temporal evolution following a quantum event, building on the TN framework. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method by applying it to the study of temporal correlation decay in an excited state, influenced by its initial, approximately entangled form. Additionally, we find that the proposed approach can capture correlation phenomena even in systems that exhibit many-body interactions, such as spin-boson models. Notably, our method shows its potential for experimental implementation using the standard tensor network simulation strategies, such as DMRG and iTEBD.

A critical factor in the effectiveness of model-based optimization methods, such as Model Predictive Control (MPC), is the quality of their parameter estimates. Adversarial attacks can disrupt the estimation process by impairing sensor measurements, compromising system visibility. In response to such threats, the practice of restricted efficacy is employed, where an attacker modulates sensor readings to mislead the controller while limiting the amplitude of the injected noise. This paper focuses on the scale-oriented aspect of this attack, where the attacker adjusts sensor inputs according to the system's state magnitude. Our aim is to investigate the implications of this advanced attack on the estimation process and to explore innovative methods to counter it through the development of scale-oriented filters. This filter development process is complicated by the absence of robust stability metrics and accurate state trajectory predictions due to the unknown attack characteristics. To address these challenges, we first establish conditions for the boundedness of states and system uncertainties. Next, we design a feedforward filter to estimate the attack impact, followed by the development of an inverse filter to predict the system's response to the attack. This prediction is then used in a sliding window approach to approximate the state trajectory. Building on this understanding, we explore the potential for generalizing this filter to counter more complex scale-oriented attacks.

In this research, we establish a new inequality that mirrors the Minkowski inequality in a non-isotropic context. To derive this inequality, we first develop an alternative approach to the classical Bogdan-Kalton-Lu-Zeep article, specifically by showing that a particular non-isotropic modification of the Minkowski inequality is a direct consequence of a broader, more generalised inequality. Building upon this foundation, we then demonstrate that the broader, generalised inequality is equivalent to another, closely related inequality. Notably, this new inequality exhibits a'reversed' structure that bears a resemblance to the relationship between the Minkowski inequality and the isoperimetric inequality. It follows from this connection that the'reversed' inequality is a non-isotropic analogue of the classical isoperimetric inequality. Furthermore, we prove that this new inequality is a direct consequence of a non-isotropic'reverse' Holder inequality.

The Microscope space test for the weak equivalence principle involves measuring tiny differences in the acceleration of two test masses as they orbit the Earth. To achieve this, the experiment relies on a 0.1 millipascal sensitivity threshold for its laser interferometer. This project encountered over 200 non-random spikes during its 630 days of operation, lasting between 0.2 seconds to a minute and a half. These glitches significantly impact the experiment's ability to make a precise weak equivalence principle measurement, potentially setting a limit at a level of $10^{-15}$ or even higher.

The surface of active microswimmers exhibits complex and diverse patterns of activity that can influence the movement of surrounding colloidal particles in various ways. This research focuses on active surfaces with activity that gradually lessens as you move further away from the center, exhibiting a linear or a quadratic decline. Our studies reveal that these active surfaces can create distinct activity gradients that can either hinder or aid the movement of colloidal particles, potentially causing them to become trapped in stable orbits around the active surface. The research also shows that the dynamics of these particles can be controlled through adjustments to the viscosity of the surrounding fluid and the surface's activity characteristics. This control can switch the particles' motion between being bounded by the surface and being freed to move unimpeded. This newfound understanding of active surfaces with complex activity patterns of this kind may find applications in the development of passive swimmers and could provide insight into the intricate interplay between active and passive components in suspensions of actively swimming particles.

The minimum strong shortest path cover with k-hops in a graph G is the smallest number of sets needed among all k-hops strong shortest path covers, and we have determined this value for certain types of graphs, including those with specific connectivity and ordering. Additionally, we have found the minimum number of k-hops strong shortest path covers for certain types of planar graphs, and we discuss the general approach used to find this value.

The impact of infrared renormalons in the color dipole gluon distribution's variance is being quantified, and calculations demonstrate how this impact influences the prediction of hadron production in proton-proton collisions at small-$x$. Specifically, the analysis examines the effect on measured quantities, such as double-differential cross-sections of proton-proton collisions leading to dihadron jettopy, $pp \to d\Delta jet \Delta jet$. A notable outcome is that the expected kT-broadening observed in such measurements can be explained by an infrared renormalon in the color dipole TMD PDF at very small $k_T \ll 1$ GeV, and that this explanation is independent of $x$ within the measured range. Furthermore, the analysis suggests that an infrared renormalon in the color dipole TMD PDF is responsible for the currently observed overestimation of jet production in proton-proton collisions at small $x \sim 0.01$, and that this discrepancy can be resolved with a more precise understanding of the parton's internal structure.

As the size of the lattice increases without limit, the probability of a particle being present in the frog model on a d-dimensional integer lattice somehow simplifies to reflect the underlying structure of an infinite tree. This complex simplification allows the model's behavior to be understood in a more manageable way, and it turns out that the resulting model is essentially a system of independent, randomly activated automata processes occurring within the infinite tree's infinite number of infinite subgraphs. This correspondence ultimately reveals that the critical density at which the frog model's particles become infinitely distant from each other is equal to the specific density required to guarantee that every point within the infinite tree is visited by a particle.

Researchers are focusing on the interconnection between photonic and magnetic properties to create novel functions, like ultrafast magnetic optics. A unique phenomenon known as magnetic photonic mode interaction affects this union. Though extensively studied in bulk materials, there's a lack of in-depth analysis for surface and lattice structures. This study delves into the examination of a unique orientation-sensitive magnetophotonic surface lattice found in Co/GaN Schottky interfaces. It utilizes a combination of magnetic and optical characterization to uncover its extraordinary capabilities. It's been discovered that this structure exhibits remarkable light-polarization dependence and directional features. As a result, it can serve as an exceptional optical mode selector and isolator. Moreover, simulations indicate that it's possible to design more intricate and high-performing devices using this kind of magnetophotonic technology.

Knowledge accumulation in various tasks constitutes a significant knowledge transfer problem that we're addressing through a zero-shot knowledge transfer framework. The key challenge lies in determining why certain models excel over others at specific tasks. Our research reveals that a well-rounded set of base models can indeed facilitate zero-shot knowledge transfer and achieve comparable performance to a task-specific model on certain tasks. We further found that models performing exceptionally well can actually impede ZSLT by diluting the necessary knowledge that's uniquely possessed by these models. Building upon this discovery, we propose an innovative framework that can identify and fine-tune models that excel at particular tasks through a black-box approach. As a result, our framework demonstrates superior performance compared to a one-to-one model matching approach in our experiments.

Researchers have observed the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 K^0_L$ decay mode for the first time, and have also gathered evidence for the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} K^0_L$ decay mode, utilizing a 3.0 $\text{fb}^{-1}$ dataset of $pp$ collisions collected at 7 and 8 TeV center-of-mass energies by the LHCb. The branching fractions for these decays are calculated as follows: The $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^0 \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is estimated at (4.3±0.5±0.3±0.3±0.6) ×10^-4, and the $B^0_s\to\bar{D}^{*0} \bar{K}^0$ branching fraction is estimated at (2.8±1.0±0.3±0.2±0.4) ×10^-4, with the given uncertainties stemming from various sources.

Constructing the lattice of submodules of a given module is generally a challenging task, however when the module in question is multiplicity-free, its associated lattice of submodules exhibits certain characteristics that make its construction more manageable. This paper focuses on providing a framework and associated algorithms for building the lattice of submodules of a free module over a commutative ring with no zero divisors, when the lattice of submodules of a corresponding quotient module is known. While the framework is conceptual, the algorithms have been implemented in Python and form the basis for further research into the properties of free modules and their associated lattices of submodules.

A strong geodetic subset of a graph connects specific nodes whose nearest neighbors are all connected to each other. Researchers refer to identifying these connections as the strong geodetic identification problem. In this study, we examine the difficulty of solving this problem when we have limited information about the graph's connections. Our main finding is that if we don't know the graph's full structure, the strong geodetic identification problem becomes extremely challenging, even in relatively simple graphs. On the other hand, if we do have access to the graph's full structure, we can solve the strong geodetic identification problem efficiently. Our main finding also extends to certain types of graphs that have a special property, known as the class of partial graphs with a specific structure, and we demonstrate that the strong geodetic identification problem can be solved efficiently for some of these types. However, our results indicate that not all types of these graphs make the strong geodetic identification problem easy to solve even when we have access to the graph's full structure.

We introduce Trail, an efficient imitation learning algorithm that surpasses
the limitations of traditional supervised learning methods. Trail leverages a
robust understanding of strong supervision - specifically, the knowledge that
having precise labels for every action significantly enhances performance. By
building on this understanding, Trail creates a strong baseline for comparison
with more complex models, like Tasseled Cap transformation-based approaches.
The innovative aspect of Trail lies in its ability to effectively utilize weak
supervision, learning from incomplete labels for every action. By doing so, it
achieves a balance that allows it to efficiently utilize strong supervision when
it is available, thus maximizing its benefits. The code for Trail is publicly
available and has been included in the repository provided.

Machine learning models excel at interpreting and drawing inferences from data but may struggle with other tasks such as data collection or observing a situation in order to make inferences. In many real-world scenarios, experts are able to observe situations and generate data that models can learn from, but they may not be able to explicitly articulate the underlying reasoning behind their observations. In such cases, models can make significant errors when relying solely on the data generated by these experts. In response to this issue, we propose a novel approach called "co-observation learning" in which models and experts alternate between observing and making inferences from data. During these interactions, models can learn to accurately replicate the expert's inferences and, as a result, generalize to new situations even if they are not seen during training. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through a series of experiments, showing that it allows models to leverage the expertise even if the data is noisy, and even learns to improve the expert's own abilities. We also explore the theoretical advantages of this approach and show that it allows models to learn from a weaker form of supervision known as "implicit supervision."

This paper provides a geometric interpretation of a code's error correction capability, which can be calculated using the distance between a code's manifold and a sphere, especially for a class of codes known as partial alternating cycle codes. The paper also presents an efficient method for determining the minimum distance between a code's manifold and another given manifold. The minimum distance can also be determined for a class of code whose manifold has a specific underlying structure. The paper's findings can be applied to a type of code known as polar alternating cycle codes.

The replacement model approach has achieved significant success in neural machine translation, but a major limitation of current methods is the excessive computational expense associated with beam search. Our proposed solution is to treat beam search as an extensive action space problem and suggest several computationally efficient strategies for search that can be learned through reinforcement learning. We evaluate and compare eight variants of search strategies and demonstrate that several of these can achieve translation accuracy on par with the standard beam search at a substantially reduced computational cost. When integrating our methods into a sequence-to-sequence summation translation model, we find that the models we propose are not only more efficient but also produce more fluent translations of difficulty cases.

A crucial aspect of collaborative robot systems is the accurate calibration without the need for external guidance or markers. The present research focuses on automating the process of calibrating a robot using a built-in depth camera without the use of external references or markers. Initially, a model is proposed to predict the position of the end-effector's tip by leveraging a unique image feature extracted from the depth camera's feed. The proposed system consists of two modules: one is a monolithic approach and the other is a distributed system. The former combines a feedforward neural network and an inverse kinematics algorithm to estimate the end-effector's position directly. The latter, on the other hand, employs a feedforward neural network to predict the robot's joint angles, which are then used in an inverse kinematics algorithm to estimate the end-effector's position. Both systems are tested using a simulated environment and an actual robot setup, and their performance is evaluated with and without initial estimates of the robot's joint angles. The results show that providing the joint angles improves the accuracy of the estimation in both systems. The proposed models are compared to a traditional approach that utilizes optical markers, and the advantages of the new methods are highlighted. The research demonstrates the potential of using a built-in depth camera to adjust and position a robot end-effector through machine learning techniques.

Quantum financial networks represent a hybrid of quantum and conventional systems, characterized by their own unique dynamics and potential for profit. In this paper, we explore the performance of a variable quantum financial system, which we term QFS-area, as it undergoes stochastic market fluctuations. Initial findings suggest that this variable QFS exhibits an interesting dual nature, displaying both stable and unstable behavior in response to changing market conditions. Analysis of its characteristics is also presented in this study.

The consumption of online news is influenced by several factors including geographical location, political views, and online behavior. This study focuses on the impact of political beliefs on online news consumption patterns. A web scraping project was implemented to analyze over 1 million online comments made on news articles spanning 20 years, covering three presidential election cycles in the United States. The results revealed a significant shift in online news consumption habits based on political affiliation, with the divide increasing substantially leading up to the most recent election. Notably, research has shown that consumers with liberal viewpoints tend to engage more actively in online discussions than those with conservative views. Furthermore, Google search data analyzed over a decade highlights distinct patterns in search queries correlated with political affiliation, with some news outlets consistently aligning with the preferences of one affiliation over the other.
We examine the properties of the word metric, specifically its growth and the complexity of the group's generators, within the rational Thompson group V.

The quantum IT backbone is built upon sequences of quantum operations performed on isolated qubits that are periodically connected to a heat bath for rejuvenation. Understanding how a driven qubit systems behave in between rejuvenations is therefore crucial. Typically, this involves dealing with a continuous stream of laser pulses that can either be random or follow a set pattern, either way it always results in a steady state of the system, often likened to a equilibrium state. In this study, we examine the scenario where the driving force is irregular, specifically when it varies in accordance with a mulitple pulse structure, and we derive a method to accurately describe this complex scenario using a system's response to a series of short, high intensity pulses, when the time between them is sufficiently long compared to a system's relaxation time. We went further and solved the steady state problem for two-level systems driven by a series of lambda pulses, and found that various combinations of pulse angles can result in a steady state that is similar to that of an equilibrium state, or lead to a situation where the system's state is constantly alternating between two states, a phenomenon that cannot occur in a system that is equilibrium-based. The method we developed can also be applied to any arbitrary pulse structure.

We explore how two distinct differential operators, denoted $X^\perp$ and $\Delta$, influence biharmonic hypersurfaces $M^n$ within the $n+2$ dimensional Euclidean space $\mathbb{R}^{n+2}$. Our research reveals that if a hypersurface satisfies specific conditions related to these operators, it ultimately meets the criteria for minimal surfaces. Furthermore, we derive key implications for the eigenvalues and characteristic functions in relation to the Ricci flow and stability of these hypersurfaces.

A continuous distribution $Q$ among $p$ distinct points $x_1, \ldots, x_p$ relative to a ratio $q$ is considered $q$-identifiable if knowing the values of $Q(x_i)/Q(x_j)$ for all pairs $i$ and $j$ allows us to determine $Q$ up to a scalar factor. The term $q$-identifiable applies to any set $X$ that can be mapped one-to-one onto the set of the $p$ distinct points $x_1, \ldots, x_p$ by a monotonic function $f$. The purpose of this paper is to explore $q$-identifiable settings for continuous distributions on $X$ and to establish basic results about it. Specifically, it has been shown that any continuous distribution on $X$ can be determined up to a scalar factor if we have access to the values of the ratio of the distribution for all pairs of points in $X$. Moreover, it is demonstrated that if the monotonic mapping $f$ from $X$ to the $p$ distinct points $x_1, \ldots, x_p$ is twice differentiable, then the $q$-identifiable $X$ sets include those for which the derivative $f'$ never equals zero and does not change sign over $X$. The paper also investigates the issue of minimum entropy for identifiable distributions on various settings and identifies an identical formula for minimum

The axion's minimal physical characteristics can be used to derive constraints on its interactions with neutrinos. By considering a system where neutrinos possess non-zero masses but no other characteristics, we can determine the minimum requirements for the axion's physical presence. In this scenario, the theory of quantum gravity holds significant influence over the neutrino's minimum mass, with the GUT scale making the system unacceptably light. Conversely, the presence of a sub-GeV scale "kicking" energy, which is associated with a particular type of heavy matter, can make the system's neutrino mass non-zero without requiring the presence of axions. This occurs as the kicking energy directly impacts the neutrino's mass, thus satisfying the minimum requirements set by the theory of quantum gravity. The implications of this theory can be observed in the production of neutrinos during the decay of heavy matter and in the process known as "leptogenic explosion" which occurs when heavy matter transforms into neutrinos and other particles. The theory also predicts that even if neutrinos have non-zero masses, they may not have the same characteristics as the axions produced during the leptogenic explosion, specifically in situations where the kicking energy exceeds the mass of heavy matter by at least two times. The theory further suggests that even if the axion is detectable in a laboratory setting, it may not be present in a particular process that involves neutrinos. The theory also raises the possibility that the characteristics of neutrinos may differ in a particular

Between 2012 and 2018, the LAMOST performed 221 observing runs and collected 5.5 terabytes of data, including  6049 exposures with a time frame of less than 7 days. Analyzing four $k$2 plates, we discovered 21 new variable stars with a range of magnitudes and periods. Among them, six are double-mode RR Lyrae candidates, 11 are single-mode RR Lyrae, three are semi-regular variable stars, and one is an eclipsing binary. The research showcases LAMOST's time-domain capabilities and its potential for discovering variable stars across the sky.

In recent years, Edge-Gated Convolutional Neural Networks (EG-CNNs) have been successful in processing volumetric images in 3D semantic segmentation tasks. Building upon the foundation of our previous work, we further explore the edge-gating mechanism and incorporate a feature refinement process to enhance training stability and output precision. This improved framework is then applied to the segmentation of brain tumors from MRI images, and our results indicate it achieves superior performance compared to the original EG-CNNs. Notably, our modified network exhibits improved performance even when trained with a significantly reduced dataset.

This paper proposes a framework for validating the transactional capabilities of NewSQL systems, including MongoDB with version 5 and later, that support multi-document atomic transactions. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework, several test scenarios were developed to ensure the validity of MongoDB's transactional features. As a result, the framework validated the correct functioning of MongoDB's transactions according to the specified requirements. However, it was found that certain features of MongoDB's transactions do not behave as expected, particularly in scenarios involving concurrent operations and data updates within a single document.

Using the elementary symmetric polynomials in variables $x_1,\dots,x_n$, we define an embedding of the space of homogeneous polynomials of degree $r$ in $n$ variables, denoted as $\Lambda_{r,n}$, where $r\leq n$. We specifically examine $\Lambda_{r,r}$ and discover that for $r\geq 5$, the image of the chromatic symmetric polynomials under this embedding does not have a nonnegative expression in the basis of monomial symmetric polynomials. This result extends our previous finding showing the nonnegative expression of these images for $r\leq 4$. Moreover, we observe that the inverse Kostka matrix exhibits a similar pattern of nonnegative entries for $r\geq 5$, providing a different explanation for the $e$-positivity of the chromatic symmetric polynomials in this case.

In the final stage of few-shot learning, relabeling and resampling perceptions from the support set and query set can significantly impact classification performance. To rectify mislabeled or insufficient samples in the support set, a novel Hindsight Summarization technique is proposed to produce a representative subset of high-quality samples for the target category through a contrastive value strategy. The proposed method aims to resample and relabel perceptions by filtering out noisy data in both the support and query sets via a two-stage filter-and-supervise approach, facilitated by Hindsight Summarization. Experimental results demonstrate that our method excels at reducing errors, enhancing data diversity, and effecting substantial performance enhancements on diverse few-shot learning scenarios and datasets.

The deployment of deep learning models, particularly those using convolutional neural networks (CNN), is frequently hampered by their inherent predisposition to favor certain image characteristics over others. This research aims to flag such inherent preferences in pre-trained medical image classification models. In a comprehensive evaluation, we examined 13 diverse publically accessible medical image datasets to determine the extent to which these preferences are unique to individual models or are a common trait among medical image classifiers. The developed framework is adaptable and enables the identification of potential biases in both natural and artificially generated medical image datasets. It is also capable of pinpointing the specific patterns or anatomical features associated with these biases.

We investigate a unique, triad-based assembly where individual particles are Ising models, interacting not only in pairs but also within equilateral triangles. By applying an exact transformation, we transform this complex system into an equivalent, two-dimensional Ising model featuring unique boundary conditions. Our analysis focuses on the distinct phenomenon of spontaneous symmetry breaking, where the triad assembly exhibits irreversible reversal dynamics due to the interaction within the equilateral triangle. Our study reveals that this occurrence is a non-equilibrium phenomenon, resulting from the unusual boundary conditions that cannot be explained by pairwise interactions alone. Moreover, our findings indicate that the reversal process is influenced by the spatial arrangement of the triads, following a power-law distribution. Additionally, we observe that the degree of spatial disorder affects the critical slowing-down phenomenon during the reversal process, providing a framework for further experimental study of this phenomenon.

The solar breeze, a continuous flow of energy and momentum from the Sun, is a vital force shaping the inner heliosphere. Utilizing data from the Parker Solar Probe, we have, for the first time, measured significant variations in the solar breeze's speed and density near the Sun's surface, specifically within 24.26 solar radii of the Sun. Our analysis reveals that high-speed solar breezes are characterized by both lower densities and cooler temperatures compared to their slow-speed counterparts. This distinction in temperatures was found to be as high as 100,000 Kelvin, with a significant 1.5 EUV brightness difference, and was observed for both the approach and recess phases of the Parker Solar Probe's mission. This understanding of the solar breeze has important implications for our understanding of the inner heliosphere and may need to be incorporated into future missions, such as the Solar Probe Plus, to ensure accurate and high-resolution observations of the solar breeze.

Speech emotion recognition, a crucial component in human-computer interaction, is not yet fully effective due to ongoing challenges. While significant progress has been made using deep learning methods, there remains a notable gap when transferring techniques from recorded data to real-world applications. In particular, adapting models to work effectively in everyday environments despite being trained on a differently formatted dataset is a key issue. These challenges stem in part from the fact that recorded data is often obtained under controlled conditions, which can distort the natural distribution of speech emotions in these settings. As a result, models trained on such data often struggle with real-world speech emotion recognition tasks. To address this, we conduct an experiment involving the adaptation of a model trained on the IEMOCAP database to perform speech emotion recognition in real-world audio. While achieving an impressive 41.75% accuracy gap reduction, our results demonstrate the potential for successful domain adaptation using both supervised and unsupervised techniques.

We present a study of Aurivillius Bi$_5$FeTi$_3$O$_{15}$ performed under high-pressure conditions, utilizing nuclear forward scattering to examine magnetic properties and lattice behavior. By measuring proton and oxygen NMR intensities under different pressures up to 24 GPa, we find magnetic long-range order occurs abruptly at 7.5 K in all pressure intervals except 0.5 GPa, where his order is absent. High-pressure structural analysis via Raman spectroscopy discloses no significant changes in the Aurivillius structure until 20 GPa, where we observe a phase transition indicated by a notable shift in the symmetric mode at 570 cm$^{-1}$. Notably, this phase transition is avoided at pressures below 0.5 GPa, where we find magnetic order is lost.

The concept of the discrete-continuous shortest path has been widely adopted in various optimization problems, but its effectiveness is significantly impaired by the error it introduces, particularly the duality gap. A new method has been developed to quantify the boundedness of this error, measured as a function of the largest possible variation in the marginal costs. The proposed approach has been demonstrated to provide a more precise error estimate than existing methods, and this improvement has been illustrated through a discrete-continuous shortest path application involving the optimization of a free flight path. The new method has been shown to provide a more accurate error bound than traditional approaches, and this error bound has a proportional relationship with the largest possible variation in the marginal costs, which has a direct impact on the design of free flight trajectories.

Researchers have previously suggested a multicomponent model of the universe, comprising matter-energy and a cosmological constant, to be the most plausible theory. Focusing on a model where the universe's matter-energy component is homogeneous, we investigated the shock wave's behavior at its boundary. We found that the shock wave's temperature varies in accordance with the $T \propto a^{-2}$ law, while displaying characteristics of both adiabatic and isothermal behavior. The analysis of the cavity's temperature, however, shows a distinct divergence from this law, resulting in the shock wave exhibiting a mixed adiabatic and isothermal profile. This distinction arises due to the differences in how the cavity's temperature is affected by the expansion of the universe, in comparison to the shock wave itself. This phenomenon may provide a means to test the validity of this universe model through the observation of shock-heated gas within galaxy clusters.

Alkan, Yucel, and Unlu introduced a new class of time-1 periodic potentials in the one-dimensional Schrodinger equation with scattering properties, based on generalized Hermite polynomials. In this work, we offer a more general framework that expands their findings to a broader family of periodic potentials derived from generalized Laguerre polynomials. By analyzing the underlying Sturm-Liouville theory, we demonstrate that these potentials meet the required criteria by demonstrating the monotonicity of the discrete spectrum and the absence of accumulation points. Furthermore, we establish a more flexible approach to generating these potentials by utilizing a non-obvious symmetry of the system. This strategy is exemplified through the construction of a new, monodromy-free Schrodinger equation with a quasi-periodic potential that resembles the famous rational normal function.

The consistent pattern of a sound produced by an adhesive tape unrolling has been the subject of limited research. This study is the first comprehensive investigation of this phenomenon, focusing on the auditory experience created as the tape unspools. Our main finding is that the pattern of sound emanating from the tape is not random but rather follows a predictable sequence of events. This sequence is influenced by the tape's unwinding mechanism and the consistent pattern of sound is a result of a self-sustaining oscillatory movement triggered by the uncoiling of the tape. This oscillatory movement is further exacerbated by the tape's increasing velocity as it unspools, creating a progressive escalation of sound intensity. Another notable aspect of this phenomenon is the emergence of a higher frequency sound pattern towards the end of the tape unrolling. This study consists of both analytical and experimental components, with the latter involving the use of high-speed cameras and microphones to collect data.

We examine the varying amplitude and phase dynamics in both planar junctions and superconducting quantum interference devices, and explain how their ac behavior is connected. Both theoretical models and numerical simulations are used in our analysis. The used theoretical model incorporates the effects of capacitance, resistance, and inductance, and is based on the Tsukuda and Takaya framework. In our study, we consider two main regimes characterized by distinct current-carrier lifetimes: in one regime, the mean lifetime is much longer than the critical time period, and in the other regime, the lifetime is significantly shorter. Our findings reveal that the phase-dynamics category determines the devices' ac behavior. When the lifetime is much longer than the critical time period, the phase-dynamics category is irrelevant, and the devices' behavior is identical. Conversely, when the lifetime is significantly shorter, the devices' behavior differs based on their phase-dynamics, and we observe both stable and unstable oscillations. Notably, in this latter regime, the Tsukuda and Takaya model fails to predict the correct current in the regime bounded by the steady-state and bifurcation points.

The Spinning Particle Model encompasses the standard model and gravitation, as demonstrated through its consistency with cosmological observations from the early universe to the present day. However, a peculiar non-abelian term exists within the model's Lagrangian, which has not been thoroughly explored despite its significance. Within this research, the ether-like term is reinterpreted in a thermal context, and its impact is examined among particle physics and cosmology communities. To facilitate this understanding, a simpler, equivalent representation of the term is introduced. Furthermore, a distinction is made between its direct effect and indirect consequences on the universe's evolution. A notable outcome of this investigation is the prediction of a distinct, thermally driven process affecting neutrinos and certain other particles, which has a more profound effect when the universe's temperature was higher.

This research develops a model that incorporates the dynamic delta hedging process of options into a framework for calculating option collateral, taking into account both option price movements and hedging expenses. By assuming that the behavior of underlying asset prices can be described by a normal mixture model, the model's options pricing component is derived, leading to the formulation of an expected value approach for calculating collateral. Given the complexity of directly computing this expectation, a more manageable expression is obtained by differentiating the options price with respect to a specific parameter, resulting in a tractable form for numerical evaluation. This form demonstrates the advantages of a flexible parametric specification, enabling the generation of collateral values through straightforward calculation. Furthermore, the model's hedging component is approximated by applying a local delta approximation, which links delta values to the underlying asset's price and facilitates the examination of how changes in asset price influence delta and, in turn, collateral calculations. A numerical example, involving options on an equity index future, illustrates the model's applicability and demonstrates the significance of considering hedging expenses in the calculation of collateral, which can exceed the cost of the option itself.

This research focuses on the long-term behavior of a variety of materials with varying levels of contrast within a rapidly changing permeability field. The underlying structure consists of a thin, high-contrast interface that separates two distinct regions of significantly different physical properties. The goal of this study is to investigate the impact of an interface that exhibits differential behavior on a wide range of problems, particularly those described by equations like Darcy's law and the porous elastic equations. Key limitations on the interface's behavior include a finite length, a periodic pattern, and a meandering curve. Our findings show that, depending on the specific limitations, the material's long-term behavior may be accurately represented by a modified set of equations that ignores the effects of the interface. Notably, the homogenization technique allows for the retention of complex dynamic forces that result from the interface's movement.

We undertook a statistical investigation of large early-type galaxies with tidal features using the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program. Our analysis focused on bright objects within $i<24.5$ across three fields, with a detected population of 2349 galaxies. We established a method to measure the fraction of light emanating from tidal structures around these galaxies, found to be $\langle f_{\rm tidal} \rangle \approx 0.006$ across all stellar mass ranges. This fraction was found to increase with tidal feature brightness relative to the galaxy's brightness, yet remained a relatively small indicator. We developed a model to predict merger rates within a given mass range based on the fraction of light from tidal features, showing that $\rm dN_{\rm merger}/\rm dT \propto T_{\rm tidal}^{-1.5}$, with $T_{\rm tidal}$ defined as the tidal feature brightness relative to the galaxy's brightness. This result may be interpreted as a prediction that major mergers among large early-type galaxies occur relatively rarely, with a rate of approximately 0.006 over a 10 billion year cosmic timeline.

A social mobility theory suggests that children's career prospects are influenced by the position of their parents, with those in higher status households having greater opportunities to advance. This model is dynamic, meaning that the chances of moving up or down in social standing are based on the current social hierarchy. We examine how opportunities are allocated within this framework, particularly focusing on the mechanisms driving intergenerational advancement and why they result in a dynamic rather than a static social structure. By exploring different methods of assigning opportunities, we find that those that emphasize personal achievement and a degree of randomness are necessary for a dynamic model of social mobility. These components help prevent a fixed class system by allowing individuals to overcome their parents' social standing and also enable those from lower status households to have opportunities to advance. Furthermore, we find that a smaller, critical mass of high-status households is necessary for a dynamic model to exhibit persistent inequality.

In the context of the energy sector, laser technology holds significant potential, with amplitude-shift-keying (ASK) being a widely adopted modulation technique. However, ASK's limited performance capabilities make 16-QAM (a more efficient modulation method) necessary for achieving high power levels. While 16-QAM can be efficiently converted back to ASK for use in power amplifiers, this process can introduce non-linear effects that compromise system performance. Given this challenge, this research focuses on designing a 2 GW-class, 1.75 $\mu$m wavelength 16-QAM system. To achieve this goal, existing laser systems were studied, with reverse engineering revealing the underlying structure and operating parameters, including temperature and voltage controls. Enhancements were then made to the temperature control mechanism to prevent thermal-induced distortions and ensure stable operation. Furthermore, numerical modeling validated the designed system's performance, showing minimal spectral and eye diagram changes when compared to the initial 1 GW-class prototype. Building upon previous work, this research demonstrates the feasibility of scaling high-power laser systems to multiple GW classes.

We demonstrate that for any given $1 < p \neq 2$ and any given $\delta > 0$, there exist quantifiable instances of $n$-dimensional $\ell_p$ spaces, denoted as $U$, such that for any isometric linear map $T$ from $\ell_p$, where the isomorphic dimension decrease ratio is greater than $\delta$, it follows that there exists an $\epsilon$-isometric linear subspace $W$ within $\ell_p$, with a dimension of at most $n$ and a $\ell_p$ unit ball that, under the application of $T$, results in a space that is greater than $\epsilon$-isometric from $W$. This theory builds upon previous research by D. K. Arora, L. Minkowski, and N. K. Shami for the case when $p=2$ and the case when $p \neq 2$.

As a tank instrument, a beam monitor like a scanning system plays a crucial role in the safe and effective operation of a particle accelerator. Capable of providing rapid feedback on beam characteristics, it also participates in the training of sophisticated real-time beam monitoring systems. Like other critical components, a scanning system requires precise calibration to ensure its accuracy and effectiveness. Unfortunately, a common challenge facing these systems is the lack of a universally accepted calibration method. To address this issue, we propose a widely applicable method for calibrating and evaluating a scanning system that is both efficient and cost-free.
