Unfortunately, there is a lack of systematic assessment available to guide future research in this field, partly due to the diverse origins of the underlying applications. Here, we initiate a systematic analysis to facilitate further research, focusing on key aspects such as network characteristics, parameters, and their relationships to the underlying taxa, processes, and other variables. To support other researchers in this field, we also outline potential research questions and outline our work's online repository of associated materials.

In observing the behavior of animals in videos, there are often subtle movements indicative of an animal's presence that may not be visible to the naked eye. To refine our understanding of these creatures and the ecosystems they inhabit, it is essential to develop a method for accurately detecting their movements automatically. This paper presents a novel approach to detecting the movement of plants and animals by analyzing changes in brightness within predefined regions of a video. The proposed algorithm was successfully applied to a range of species, including insects that remain invisible to the human eye, and yielded highly reliable detection results.

Matrix inversion methods can facilitate efficient response time-domain simulations in various applications including seismic imaging and electromagnetic field computations. Notwithstanding this, in-depth analysis reveals that conventional high-order finite-element method (HFEM) simulations suffer from slow convergence rates when employing an iterative linear solver with a minimal residual method. To circumvent this limitation, this research introduces an alternative iterative solver known as the Krylov subspace method, specifically tailored for modern GPU processing. To enhance its performance, the research proposes a strategy for preconditioning that is both efficient and straightforward to implement. Moreover, this research introduces a straightforward yet effective way to construct a highly efficient preconditioner based on an approximate inverse of a block diagonal matrix, obtained through an iterative process that leverages finite-element connectivity for optimal computational performance. Ultimately, this research demonstrates its efficacy by applying the proposed method to a high-resolution simulation of seismic wave propagation.

In systems that scatter waves, properties like absorption can be analyzed using eigenchannels, a concept closely related to the angular spectrum method. This paper introduces new tools to classify and organize eigenchannels based on their transmission and reflection properties. It identifies specific subsets of eigenchannels that maximize energy transmission or reflection, as well as absorption, and derives simple formulas to calculate the average transmission, reflection, and absorption in these subsets. The paper also explores the connection between these subsets and systems that scatter waves, particularly in the case of semi-infinite systems with interfaces. It finds that the energy absorption in these systems is maximized by eigenchannels that are perpendicular to the interface.

We examine topological Anderson insulators in one-dimensional lattice models with randomly introduced binary disorders that vary in intensity. Our research focuses particularly on models featuring on-site disorders with distinct amplitudes and a crossover from non-topological to topological characteristics induced by the disorders. Our studies on free fermions within a one-dimensional Su-Glauber model demonstrate that the topological phase can be realized when the disorder intensity exceeds a minimum threshold, regardless of the disorder's spatial arrangement. However, even when the disorder is randomly distributed, the topological regime can still be entered if the average disorder intensity exceeds a certain critical value. Our findings on interacting fermions indicate that the topological phase is more readily induced by binary disorders than by uniform disorders, and we anticipate that this will have implications for the experimental realization of topological states.

The concept of isomorphism, a fundamental equivalence between structures, has been extensively explored in various branches of mathematics. Isomorphism types can be organized into a hierarchical framework consisting of subcategories, including the category of finite structures, the category of countable structures, and numerous other specialized categories. Within the context of finite structures, the number of isomorphism types is finite, in contrast to the countable structures where the number of isomorphism types is uncountably infinite and exceeds the number of automorphism types. This research focuses on the finite structures and presents an innovative approach to identifying isomorphism types by utilizing the symmetry of structures and the concept of a trims structure. A trims structure represents a minimal representation of an isomorphism type, consisting of all possible substructures that, when combined in a specific way, result in a structure that is isomorphic to the original structure. The relationship between trims structures and isomorphism types provides a more manageable framework, allowing for an infinite number of structures to be organized in a finite two-dimensional array. This arrangement enables easy navigation and enables the confirmation of whether a specific structure falls within a particular isomorphism type. The concept of trims structures has implications beyond finite structures and suggests that a similar approach may be applicable to the broader category of structures.

The standard model's reputation as a fundamental theory is upheld by experimental evidence, yet it falls short in explaining several phenomena, thereby necessitating the introduction of a more comprehensive theory that incorporates the necessary elements of electroweak symmetry breaking, dark matter, and a suitable mediator for high-energy particle interactions. One such potential extension to the standard model is provided by supersymmetry, which assigns a minimal set of new particles to the standard model's existing ones in a way that maintains the consistency of the original theory. Supersymmetry's potential to address the standard model's shortcomings makes it worthy of further investigation, but its ability to do so depends on its ability to accurately predict the behavior of the Higgs boson, a process that involves a complex interplay of numerous variables. This study investigates the likelihood that the Higgs boson's behavior can be accurately predicted using a supersymmetric model that is based on the minimal supersymmetric standard model and incorporates a random and intricate set of variable assignments, a process that involves a large amount of data that needs to be analyzed in a comprehensive manner. In recent years, researchers introduced network autoregressive models, significantly improving forecasting performance, particularly in external evaluation scenarios. However, the limited understanding of linearity within this framework hinders its extensive adoption. To address this knowledge gap, we investigate linearity in network autoregressive models through multiple methods, including residual analysis, kernel-assisted tests, and synthetic data. Our findings indicate that non-linear network autoregressive models consistently outperform their linear counterparts. Furthermore, we observe that linear network autoregressive models can mimic the performance of their non-linear counterparts when given additional relevant information. Moreover, we discover that linearity is readily achieved by incorporating a rich network Z-matrix. Our research offers a foundational understanding of linearity within network autoregressive models and provides a theoretical basis for future research to explore more intricate specifications.

In recent years, deep declarative networks (DDNs) have gained significant interest as they offer an alternative to the traditional forward-pass training method for neural networks. Dually, our issue framework proposes making the learning process and model development processes transparent and manageable for researchers and practitioners. This framework can be applied across various types of networks, including DNNs, graph networks, and DNNs combined with program logic. We demonstrate the utility of our proposed framework by examining not just the underlying architecture of DNNs but also delving into the design of two models utilizing the framework - a declarative transformer and a declarative super-resolution model. These models not only showcase the feasibility of incorporating the issue framework into DNNs but also highlight the importance of transparent transformation functions in the learning process.

A new mathematical framework is introduced that adapts the method of differential equations for the study of living cells to incorporate key biological processes. The proposed framework builds upon existing methods by accounting for the movement of cells, the relocation of proteins on membranes and how these proteins move in response to surrounding fluid dynamics. This new structure can facilitate a broad range of computational modeling techniques, enabling both detailed examinations of cellular behavior and more general assessments that can be large-scale and computationally efficient. The introduction of this framework is demonstrated through a simple application, focusing on a scenario where cells are responding to fluid flow by moving towards areas of highest velocity.

The growing reliance on cryptocurrency-based solutions necessitates a robust security framework that can detect and comprehensively understand suspicious activity within their underlying blockchain infrastructure. While traditional anomaly detection methods can identify potential threats, they fall short in providing a thorough analysis of complex situations that could aid in further investigation and securing the system against future attacks. To address this limitation, we propose an innovative approach that not only flags suspicious transactions but also offers a detailed explanation of the underlying circumstances that led to these events, based on a combination of natural language processing and machine learning techniques. By illustrating our method's effectiveness with real-world examples from the Ethereum blockchain, our research demonstrates its capacity to effectively identify and interpret complex situations arising from various sources, including simple, mid-level, and complex circumstances. Furthermore, our approach outperforms a competing detection and comprehension system in both accuracy and comprehensiveness.

Quantum computing's potential is immense, but it's hampered by the fragile nature of quantum processors. To make practical progress, fault-tolerant quantum execution is essential. The surface code model exhibits resilient coding possibilities but demands considerable computational resources. A key challenge lies in developing efficient conversion tools that can transform the encoded information into a decipherable form. Conventionally, manual coding techniques based on deep learning have achieved remarkable success but are often impractical due to their slow speed. For instance, standard tensor network coding requires excessively long decoding sequences, rendering it ineffective. In this paper, we introduce an innovative approach, involving the application of reinforcement learning to coding, which autonomously devises sequences to extract encoded data. By integrating the coding and decoding processes, we have developed a suite of coding sequences that can be directly used for decoding without further conversion. This not only accelerates the decoding process but also enhances the overall computational efficiency. Through this novel approach, we have obtained a 10 to 100 times improvement in computational speed for various quantum simulation applications.

Quantum metrology enhances precision by leveraging the interplay of quantum states, specifically using entanglement to minimize errors. This research focuses on an uncharacterized dual-cavity network, where quantum states are shared between two separate quantum systems connected by an unknown transformation. It has been found that quantum states within this dual-cavity framework can exhibit over-entanglement, surpassing the maximum possible value when isolated. This phenomenon occurs when light interacts with a medium exhibiting high susceptibility. It has also been demonstrated that quantum states displaying this over-entanglement can provide a level of precision beyond classical limits, even without any initial information about the dual-cavity network. This over-entanglement can be achieved experimentally using only a few parameters, without the need to control or optics within the network. It further allows for the precise estimation of a high-sensitivity parameter using a single measurement, a process known as quantum leap metrology.

The production of direct photons in hadron productions has been utilized as a means to discern jet interactions with the medium in heavy-ion collisions. A thorough investigation of photon-hadron correlations in 200 GeV Au$+$Au and $d$$+$Au collisions from the PHENIX experiment has yielded significant insights into jet-medium interactions. In 0.5$~t$\le$\eta_{\gamma}$\le$1.0, photon-hadron correlations exhibit an away-side asymmetry, indicating that the jet's interaction with the medium influences its direction. Furthermore, in Au$+$Au collisions, the observed asymmetry is consistent with a median angle shift of approximately 0.0045 radians in the direction opposite to the prompt photon. The findings are in line with the concept of jet quenching and are independently confirmed by measurements of away-side dihadron asymmetry.

This paper formulates a novel mathematical concept called the universal Smarandache's sigma product of figures, establishing a connection between this idea and the Euler's totient function in relation to the prime factorization of positive integers. Additionally, it proves several theoretical findings related to the universal Smarandache's sigma product of figures and presents computational results to illustrate its practical applications.

Optimizing the performance of cloud applications is an intricate task due to the complex and dynamic nature of network performance. While the standard approach focuses solely on processing power and storage, our research explores the unseen effects of network performance on cloud applications. Through experimental and theoretical analyses, we uncovered the hidden patterns of network performance that influence cloud applications, as well as effective methods for optimizing the configuration of cloud platforms based on network performance variability. Our findings reveal the critical role of network performance in cloud applications, and we demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed methods in configuring cloud platforms for optimal performance. By leveraging these methods, cloud providers can offer high-performance applications even in the presence of network performance variability, and the associated source code is available for further modification and improvement.

In complex cooperative systems with multiple agents, the context in which they interact may convey sensitive information, thus requiring a secure framework for cooperative decision-making. This paper introduces a novel approach to a contextual linear gambit model, in which agents privately hold their individual contexts and jointly learn a cooperative policy without exchanging their internal information. This approach is mathematically represented as an optimization problem subject to constraints and is computationally feasible for a limited number of contextual samples. To overcome computational challenges for a larger number of contextual samples, a distributed algorithm is devised and proven to converge within a predetermined distance to an optimal solution. This innovative solution has been successfully applied to a linear gambit framework and demonstrated superior performance in comparative simulations to traditional cooperative algorithms.

The study explored the impact of remote working on the success of Scrum projects, investigating potential challenges and solutions through both a quantitative and qualitative analysis. A statistical examination of project data revealed a significant correlation between remote working and project success, while an in-depth interview with software developers uncovered several potential difficulties associated with remote working within a Scrum framework, including impaired communication, difficulty in estimating task duration, and increased risk of task abandonment. However, these challenges could potentially be mitigated through clear project goals, effective risk management, and regular progress assessments.

We appreciate the opportunity to respond to the thoughtful comments from seersubmitters. Our research aimed to address the challenge of developing treatment recommendations that are robust to unexpected shifts in data, by leveraging the concept of distributionally robust individualized treatment (DRIE). We demonstrated the efficacy of an optimization-based approach and a machine learning-enabled framework for creating DRIE through optimization and testing. The proposed frameworks are efficient, flexible, and yield treatments that minimize regrets under real-world data variations. Furthermore, our approach is applicable to various treatment outcomes and has been successfully evaluated through large-scale simulations, yielding DRIE with up to 25% lower regret compared to non-robust individualized treatment.

The CMS experiment at the LHC gathered data from lead-lead collisions at a 2.76 TeV collision energy, enabling a detailed study of central absolute rapidity gap distributions and underlying event components in proton-proton collisions at the same energy level. A comprehensive analysis of the data revealed a central proton-proton collision event characteristic that can be utilized in a novel manner. By employing this characteristic, a thorough examination of lead-lead collision data becomes feasible without employing bias based on jet presence, allowing for a precise investigation of elliptic motion in lead-lead collisions and a thorough examination of jet spectra in proton-proton collisions at 2.76 TeV. A notable rise in elliptic flow magnitude is observed across a broad momentum range, from 2 to 6 GeV, and a distinct ratio of elliptic flow magnitude in the light antiquark direction compared to the light quark direction is evident. Furthermore, a notable rise in elliptic flow magnitude is observed in the light quark direction beyond 3 GeV, and a distinct ratio of elliptic flow magnitude in the light antiquark direction compared to the light quark direction is evident. A notable rise in elliptic flow magnitude is observed across a broad momentum range, from 2 to 6 GeV.

This article formulates the Quaternion Linear Canonical Stockwell Transform as a linear canonical transform in the Quaternion analytic domain and proves its properties, specifically proving it satisfies properties of linearity, invertibility, and periodicity. We derived the MODL and MIDL theorems for this transform and established the relationship between the Quaternion Linear Canonical Stockwell Transform and the standard Linear Canonical Transform. The article also explores the non-répère (non-standard) property of this transform which results in an infinite number of indeterminacies for both discrete and continuous applications.

This work extends our previous research on the ultimate high-SNR benefits of continuous power optimization in multi-user interference networks. Initially, we found that when interference is present in non-VLSI networks, the benefits of continuous optimization over binary power control methods can be substantial, reaching up to $\frac{K}{2}$ in an network with a large number of users, although it may be as low as zero in some cases. Now, we are investigating the same question in a more general context, excluding cases where the capacity matrix has a specific singular value structure. Our main finding is that in an $K$ user network, the benefits of continuous optimization over binary power control can be as high as $\frac{K^{1.5}}{e^{0.5}}$ and as low as $\frac{K^{1.5}}{e^{1.5}}$. Moreover, our results demonstrate that binary spatial time-sharing is an optimal solution for many more cases than previously known. Additionally, we propose a new criterion for maximum capacity at high SNR, which is based on the strongest singular value of the normalized interference matrix.

The growing popularity of particle-resolved simulation has created a significant need for integration methods that can balance accuracy and computational efficiency. Most existing methods for simulating fluid-particle interactions employ artificial collision models with negligible durations, which, however, may lead to inaccuracies in particle motion prediction, particularly when multiple particles are present. To address this limitation, we have developed an innovative integration method that leverages time steps both much shorter than typical fluid time steps and much longer than collision time scales, enabling a more precise capture of particle motion, including when multiple particles are interacting. This method's effectiveness was demonstrated through a series of numerical experiments, including simulations of a single particle falling in a viscous fluid, particles falling through a fluid with high Reynolds numbers, and particles interacting with one another in a fluid, with excellent agreement with reference solutions generated by an exact integration method.

This article presents $2$ distinct proof methodologies establishing the existence of infinitely many pairs of relatively prime positive integers, $a$ and $b$, for which the following congruence is satisfied: the expression $a^2+ab+b^2$ can be factored as $7$ raised to a power of $n$.

The unique mobility mode of biped and triped robots that hop involves a complex
dynamic interaction between the device and its surroundings, significantly influenced
by external surfaces that deform under the robot's weight and movement. Due to the
challenging nature of modeling such environments, researchers often employ stiff
and frictionless surfaces in simulations to simplify modeling, which can result in
overestimation of the robot's performance. This research focuses on simulating and
experimenting with a single-legged hopping robot on deformable surfaces. A new
approach to modeling surface dynamics has been developed and incorporated into a
simulation framework to compare simulated results with actual test data when the
robot is operating on various types of deformable terrain. The study demonstrates
that simulated and actual measurements correlate closely, showing that surface
stiffness has a significant impact on trip height but minimal effect on hopping
frequency. Additionally, the research found that there is an optimal surface
stiffness at medium frequencies of deformation, where the robot experiences highest
elevation during movement on different types of terrain. This work has the
potential to contribute to the development of more sophisticated simulation tools
that can simulate complex terrain conditions, which is essential for optimizing the
design and operation of triped and biped robots in various environments.

In this paper, we integrate the concepts of a extended linear sigma model and a linear meson-meson effective theory to create a unified framework that can predict form factors for meson elastic scattering. The model's ability to make precise predictions for form factors is a key advantage. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that the meson's internal structure plays a significant role in determining the behavior of form factors at both low and high energy points. The model also effectively uses the concept of a "hadron volume" to explain the phenomenon of a positive slope observed in data on meson elastic scattering at high energies. The unified framework also offers a plausible explanation for the observed difference in the magnitude of the elastic scattering cross-section for different meson types. The model's parameters are also consistent with those obtained from other sources, which adds to its credibility.

When a droplet is placed between two electrodes and an electric field is applied, it starts to move and eventually settles into a stable position where it begins to oscillate rapidly, exhibiting a complex hydrodynamic behavior despite appearing simple. However, the simplicity of this setup belies the intricate dynamics at play, especially when an external influence such as an surrounding gas field is introduced. In the presence of an electric field, the droplet starts to interact with the surrounding gas in a way that affects its movement, ultimately being drawn into a self-sustaining vortex pattern due to the uneven distribution of electric field forces. This phenomenon has significant implications for the way droplets behave in the atmosphere, particularly when they are subjected to the influence of an external field.

Effective communication through language cannot exist without the concept of negation, which conveys the opposite meaning of affirmation.  Despite being a fundamental aspect of language, studying the implications of negation remains underdeveloped in comparison to other language topics. To bridge this knowledge gap, we need a diverse and extensive dataset that includes contexts where negation is used. We have created CONDAQA, a diverse reading comprehension dataset that requires reasoning about negation to arrive at the correct answer. It consists of 10,000 multiple-choice questions based on articles from the Wikipedia web portal. These questions are designed in a way that test a model's ability to understand the implications of negation used in the context. We have implemented two indicators - one that assesses a model's capacity to understand the implications of a single negated statement, and the other that evaluates a model's capacity to understand the effects of multiple negated statements within a single context. We have conducted various experiments to evaluate the performance of different machine learning models on CONDAQA, and our results demonstrate the challenges posed by this dataset, highlighting the significant disparity between models that can learn from large volumes of training data and those that can understand the implications of negation from limited information. We have also observed that negation can sometimes have the opposite effect, and we have included additional research to explore this phenomenon. We believe that CONDAQA will serve as a valuable resource to enhance the understanding of machine learning models in relation to language that involves negation.

The analysis of complex networks using graph algorithms is a key in various disciplines, but a significant obstacle many face is the need to calculate a preliminary reduction of the network before more in-depth analysis can begin. A novel method was developed which allows for the direct computation of multiple structures within a single pass through the network, utilizing a general framework that can be applied to diverse types of networks and nodes with multiple attributes. This approach was successfully applied to several real-world networks from different domains, demonstrating its effectiveness and efficiency. A available implementation of the method can be explored at https://github.com/aliyevk/StructR.

Quantum annealing shows considerable promise in addressing complex optimization challenges, primarily due to its capability to overcome first-order transitions that conventional annealing methods cannot overcome. Nevertheless, the likelihood of successfully employing quantum annealing depends on the annealing schedule being used, as well as the problem at hand. Research on quantum annealing dynamics is limited, and a notable absence in this field is a defined quantum annealing interval - the range within which quantum fluctuations can facilitate overcoming insurmountable transitions through quantum tunneling. This paper investigates the quantum annealing interval in model problems, including exact cover, by comparing quantum annealing and conventional quench dynamics using two distinct propagation methods. The findings indicate that quench dynamics may serve as a more reliable and direct method for determining the quantum annealing interval than quantum simulation itself. The research further reveals that the quantum annealing interval is significantly larger than the correlation length in certain circumstances, a discovery that has implications for the suitability of quench dynamics in identifying optimal annealing schedules.

The problem of verifying compliance in robotics refers to checking if a robot's actual movements match its planned trajectory. This paper focuses on this challenge for robot arms with two joints, where the task involves comparing a planned trajectory with an actual one defined by a set of line segments. In order to make this comparison, the paper introduces a new mathematical concept called infix alignment, along with an associated measure that can be optimized efficiently. However, this approach has limitations, so the paper explores two variants of the problem, one where the comparison is restricted to parts of the planned path, and another where the actual path is defined by a continuous curve. The paper also discusses the results of testing these methods on simulated data and a small-scale real-world experiment.

The unusual electronic and magnetic properties of nickelate superconductors can be understood using a dual-band model, comprising $4s$ and $3d_{x^2-y^2}$ orbitals, where a strong intra-band Coulomb interaction and electron transfer between these orbitals are present. Due to electron transfer, the normally filled 4s orbital contains some magnitude of a negative charge for, causing strong screening of the 3d orbital's Coulomb interaction. As a result, electron-hopping terms are heavily renormalized, leading to a symmetry that cannot be described by a simple two-band Hubbard model. By accounting for screening through a resonance on the 4s orbital, we demonstrate that it diminishes the complexity of the model while maintaining its essential features. Furthermore, we show that screening is responsible for the peculiar magnetic phase diagram observed, specifically the absence of a Mott-Hubbard insulating phase and the inability to independently tune the system's electron transfer and Coulomb interaction parameters.

This research investigates the long-term behavior of solutions to the non-cutoff Boltzmann equation in an infinite space, with initial conditions where the density of particles displays a gentle decline from equilibrium and a wave-like oscillation in time. As time extends, these solutions converge to a stable phase where the particle density closely resembles equilibrium, with minor random fluctuations. This convergence is marked by an early "diffusive" phase where the oscillations gradually disappear. Notably, this finding contrasts with previous outcomes for bounded frequency models, where oscillations persist indefinitely.

We utilized infrared radiation observations from space to examine the relationship between wave direction and slope over a six-year period, confirming previous research findings that used a single-day dataset, which showed a significant bias. Our analysis revealed a near-zero mean angle between wind and wave direction, approximately 5 degrees, and a relatively low standard deviation of 15 degrees. Additionally, we found a standard deviation of 20-25 degrees for the angle between wind and wave slope. Notably, our results indicated that waves were generally oriented downwind of the actual wind direction.

The growth of diverse software systems necessitates flexible and efficient testing, involving the selection of test cases that can detect faults across various inputs, including those with both discrete and continuous components. While recent studies have proposed test case selection algorithms, they primarily focus on specific systems and lack consideration for parallel processing. Recent research on unique value decomposition (UVD) offers an efficient way to generate unique combinations of variables, but does not address the challenges posed by complex systems with a wide range of input variables. Building on our previous work on UVD-based test case selection, we have developed an enhanced method to tackle system complexity, incorporating parallel processing to speed up the test case selection process.

Social media platforms can provide valuable insights into public emotions during significant events, but often limit access to statistical data. Twitter remains an exception, allowing researchers to analyze a wide range of aspects of the emotions expressed by the public using Twitter posts about the COVID-19 outbreak. In this research, a specialized dataset was created to focus on the emotions expressed during the initial pandemic wave, when lockdown measures were enforced. By applying multiple classification methods to 300,000 Twitter posts from the dataset, the prevalence of public emotions was mapped, revealing how they varied over time and across different topics. Notably, people expressed greater anxiety when discussing the pandemic's health aspects and increased frustration when talking about measures to control the outbreak. Furthermore, the public's emotional response to economic aspects of the pandemic lagged behind the peak of infected cases and hospital admissions. By exploring these findings, the opportunity is also taken to discuss the challenges faced and present additional aspects of the emotions expressed during this period.

The interlayer conductivity of cuprate superconductors exhibits unique characteristics resulting from their intricate electronic structure and the competition between different microscopic processes. Due to the intricate nature of these systems, conventional models are insufficient, and a novel approach is required. This paper presents a general framework that incorporates cuprate superbases with charge density waves, enabling the derivation of an extended Uhlmann-James relation and a modified Fischer-Lee relation through the use of noncommutative geometry. This framework offers a more comprehensive understanding of interlayer conductivity and provides a basis for formulating an extended Bardeen-Stephan theory.

The adiabatic index that determines sound propagation in matter is a fundamental characteristic of matter, influencing the behavior of stars and black hole mergers. However, its value is distorted by interactions and many-body effects within dense, strangeness-rich matter, especially in the cores of neutron stars. We calculate this adiabatic index for various quark flavors, considering both non-interacting and interacting quarks, and map its relationship to the percentage of strange matter in the star. The results indicate that sound propagates differently, either correctly (1.5-2.2) or incorrectly (0.5-1.5), depending on the quark interactions, with minimal impact on the star's radius.

Phylogenetic estimation from sequence data is often hampered by the limited information contained in alignment columns that have undergone multiple substitutions. Recent methods that use labeled trees and a stochastic emission model have shown superior performance, but involve computationally demanding posterior calculations or the optimization of a complex scoring function. Adversarial training is an emergent technique that enables fast and efficient model optimization for complex objectives. We introduce an innovative use of adversarial techniques, named adverse tai mapping, that maps labeled tree topologies to the underlying phylogeny, promoting the recovery of the correct tree structure without the need for expensive posterior calculations. By integrating adverse tai mapping with a novel loss function, we propose a fast and efficient method for estimating labeled trees from sequence data. Our experiments demonstrate that this method outperforms traditional maximum likelihood methods and several modern competitors, often doing so at a significantly lower computational cost.

In quantum optics, superposed states of a harmonic oscillator, also known as Sagnac states or balanced states, have significant applications and exhibit non-classical properties. These states can be used for implementing various quantum operations and maintaining quantum communication systems. Recently, two novel methods were proposed for generating balanced states based on non-linear interactions involving a two-level system and an oscillator in a cavity. However, these proposed schemes assume that the oscillator's initial state is a vacuum state. In this study, we investigate the effectiveness of using a squeezed state as the initial state of the oscillator and examine the balanced state's quality as a function of the squeezing parameter. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using a squeezed state can yield higher balanced state fidelity compared to a vacuum state. This discovery is particularly noteworthy since squeezed states are more robust against decoherence induced by cavity losses. Moreover, we observe that applying a displacement to the vacuum state can achieve even higher balanced state fidelity than using a squeezed state. This optimization technique is highly versatile as it can be employed to achieve the highest possible balanced state overlap for both Gaussian and non-Gaussian states of the oscillator.

A significant phenomenon in protoplanetary disk systems is the vertical shear instability, characterized by the occurrence of channels or spiral structures that may play a crucial role in the development and growth of solid particles. In the outer regions of these disks, where the conditions are less extreme, a different type of instability may emerge, influenced by the development of dust grains. This paper investigates how the growth of dust affects the vertical shear instability in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks, focusing on the development of a two-dimensional disk with a varying solid content that forms gradually. The research involves a numerical simulation using the PDLAB code to analyze how the growth of dust affects the stability of the disk by modifying the viscous and Reynolds stresses, and how it impacts the channel height, amplitude, and growth rate of the instability. The findings indicate that the increase in dust content enhances the shear instability, accelerating its growth, and resulting in a more pronounced amplitude and channel height. This has implications for the development of solid particles in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks, suggesting that the vertical shear instability could be a critical process in the further growth of dust grains in these areas.

This note builds upon Liouville Theorem 1.1, establishing that a compact subset of R^n with constant mean curvature and bounded by a sphere of radius r > 0 is a distance r to the sphere. The theorem's proof will be demonstrated, followed by an exploration of its applications to the classification of embedded surfaces of constant mean curvature in R^n+.

Multi-branch networks have been successfully applied to various tasks such as classification, detection, and segmentation by providing a balanced trade-off between computational complexity and accuracy. While research has focused on selecting an optimal number of branches, little attention has been given to a fundamental issue - that of how to combine feature representations from multiple branches. In our proposed framework, we address this issue by introducing dynamic entrances with a global mean pooling layer, which allows for the flexible inclusion of both parallel branches and allows models to selectively learn from them. Experiments have demonstrated that our proposed framework not only outperforms traditional fixed multi-branch networks but also achieves comparable performance to state-of-the-art single-branch networks.

The highly accurate measurements provided by the Gaia spacecraft are significantly influenced by post-Newtonian corrections to the gravitational potential, specifically the PPN gamma parameter. It is possible to model these effects in the positions, velocities, and parallaxes of stars, albeit with a level of uncertainty. The current study assesses the impact of a non-zero gamma value on the measurement of parallaxes, employing a maximum likelihood estimator and mock Gaia data. The results indicate that a value of gamma as low as -2x10^-5 could introduce a systematic error in the determination of parallaxes, specifically in the range of a few microarcseconds. It is also found that the likelihood distribution of parallaxes is bi-modal when gamma is non-zero, effectively causing a portion of the measured parallaxes to be overestimated. The study further reveals that the most distant stars from the Sun are those most susceptible to this bias. The analysis also includes an estimate of the expected error in the determination of gamma by Gaia, which is forecasted to be in the range of a few times 10^-5. The study ultimately suggests that future parallax measurements with the aid of Gaia-like technology should be accompanied by the estimation of the PNS gamma parameter.

We have developed a powerful new approach that uses high-fidelity simulations and experiments to rapidly create simplified models that accurately capture complex behaviors. These simplified models can be used to make quick and confident predictions, even in situations where the original system becomes unstable or difficult to understand. Our approach is especially useful for creating models in multiple variables, by making them more efficient to compute and easier to grasp. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method by applying it to a variety of challenging systems, including ones with multiple variables, a mix of stable and unstable elements, and a unique layout that makes it hard to identify the key factors at play.

In one-dimensional models of nonlinear wave equations with higher-order effects, researchers have a long-standing desire to demonstrate the existence of solitons with peak amplitude that can be made self-sustaining through a minor correction, even in the absence of external influences. By developing a novel approach that incorporates an adiabatic representation and a consistent transformation technique, our study proves the existence of such self-stable solitons for the Bose-Einstein condensate model affected by quadratic dissipation and for a model of shallow water waves with a fifth-order dispersion term.

This research introduces a revised version of SIMC, a framework designed to safeguard machine learning (ML) model-sharing against malicious clients. The original SIMC framework relies on hidden layers within the ML model to detect and prevent security breaches during inference, but this study shows that a crafty user could potentially bypass its protections. In response, this research proposes enhanced features for the ML model, incorporating both hidden and active components to protect against both internal and external threats, respectively. The revised framework, dubbed SIMC 2.0, leverages the trusted hardware layer to ensure the integrity of the inference process. Furthermore, this research explores various model architecture configurations and evaluates the performance of the enhanced SIMC 2.0 framework in terms of model complexity, accuracy, and efficiency. Experimental results demonstrate that SIMC 2.0 can effectively prevent a hostile client from manipulating the inference output and offers a reliable solution for secure ML model-sharing.

New FAST observations of the M101 galaxy at 1.4 GHz have yielded a significant discovery of high-velocity HI gas clouds, with some of these clouds originating from outside the galaxy. Additionally, a previously unknown HI tail was found extending beyond the optical limits of M101. This finding may be linked to a minor collision with the nearby galaxy NGC 4603, although the exact nature and impact of this interaction require further investigation.

To effectively handle questions that require a broad range of background knowledge, as seen in commonsense question answering, several key elements must be addressed. This paper introduces a novel semantic-related question answering framework that not only considers questions with explicit clues but also those with implicit connections. To thoroughly examine these questions, a two-stage answer generation approach is employed. Initially, the framework generates a coarse answer based on a broad range of background information. If the coarse answer does not match expectations, a refined answer is then provided by focusing on related concepts. This paper presents a publicly accessible code and dataset to facilitate further research in this area.

The knowledge of how molecules form in the coma and tail of comets is enhanced by combining spectroscopic and photometric observations with simulations of the processes occurring during the passage of a comet through the inner regions of the solar system. However, the accuracy of such simulations is hindered by a lack of data on how certain molecules are formed and their abundance. This study makes use of a comprehensive model of the formation and molecular spectrum of oxygen-bearing molecules in the coma and tail of comets, particularly C2, C3, diatomic carbon-based molecules (CO, CN, CCH, CP, and CH), and the cyclopropenylidyne molecule (C3H). It shows that a more thorough understanding of the formation and molecular spectrum of these molecules is necessary in order to accurately interpret observations of comets such as C/2003 OG13 (SOHLAR) and others with low velocities.

The total of squares problem asks whether a given element in a global field can be expressed as the sum of squares. Although this problem is undecidable in general, we provide a deterministic approach for deciding whether a given element is the sum of two squares in global fields. Building on this, we also develop a method for determining whether a given element is the sum of three squares in global fields. Additionally, we investigate the sum of four squares in global fields and establish a connection to the total of squares problem in quadratic fields. Notably, if a quadratic field has a rational embedding in the given global field, we can determine whether a specific element is the sum of four squares. Furthermore, we establish conditions under which an element in a global field can be expressed as the sum of four squares using a combination of two squares from the same factor.

The rising number of discoveries in the astrophysics sector is sparking a significant surge in new sources that need their spectral characteristics cross-checked. As a result, there's a growing necessity for new methods to accurately identify and link sources that share the same coordinates, spectral features, and other properties. To address this challenge, we present three new approaches - based on photonic technology, specifically designed to efficiently tackle this issue. These methods utilize unique light patterns to create patterns of maximum and minimum values, effectively detecting features by looking for instances where the light pattern is disrupted. Furthermore, they provide a direct means of comparing sources with different spectral features, and there's potential for them to be applied to a wide range of data sets.

The precise selection of medications for optimal synergy is crucial, however, identifying interactions becomes increasingly difficult as the number of possible combinations grows, exceeding the ability of experimental methods to keep pace. While current studies using machine learning have shown promise, there is still a critical need to thoroughly examine the underlying concepts and methods employed. In this work, we offer a comprehensive review of a crucial subset of machine learning techniques, specifically relational and graph-based methods, and examine their applications to medication combination scoring. Our analysis reveals key advantages and disabilities of these techniques, as well as common challenges faced, such as the scarcity and low-quality of available data. To address these issues, we propose a framework for data curation and experimental design to facilitate more robust evaluations of ML methods. Finally, we emphasize the importance of open-source code and pre-trained models to facilitate further research and development in this domain.

The analysis of a wide range of mathematical models, including stochastic control, rough paths theory, and stochastic differential equations, heavily relies on the use of certain differential equations to analyze their solutions. This paper focuses on extending the traditional Itô equation to a more general type of stochastic process known as a $\gamma$-rough path for any $\gamma\in (0,1)$. By doing so, we establish a key result that enables the existence and uniqueness of solutions to a specific type of differential equation when the underlying stochastic process has parameters within the beta-$\beta$-Hölder class and satisfies certain continuity conditions. Additionally, this existence and uniqueness result is shown to be a key consequence of a more general differential equation known as the Itô-Wentzell equation.

The cross-validation method has been the primary approach used to address the domain shift issue in cross-domain learning, but it has significant drawbacks such as high computational costs, over-reliance on assumptions, and inefficient utilization of target domain data. Target domain data is under-represented in traditional federated learning settings due to the need for secure and private data storage, further exacerbating the domain shift issue. A new random stroll method is introduced in this paper to tackle these challenges. In the proposed framework, a random stroll model is introduced that selects a small batch size of diverse data points from the target domain with low density, allowing for efficient and secure learning without the need for data fusion. Extensive experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate that the random stroll model achieves comparable performance to the cross-validation method and outperforms other baseline methods. A theoretical analysis of the proposed algorithm is also provided, and we find that it is comparable to the cross-validation method in terms of risk bounds.

This study confirms the Zakharov-Kolmogorov spectrum in rotating shear flows by analyzing numerical simulations of three-dimensional periodic domains. The chosen test case involved a variety of rotation rates, with the spectrum being observed to transition from an inertial boundary layer-dominated spectrum at high angular momentum to a self-similar Kolmogorov-Zakharov spectrum in between the viscous boundary layers and the geostrophic condensation layer to a dominated boundary layer spectrum at low angular momentum, resembling Kyodo's (Phys. Rev. Lett., vol. 127, 2021) experimental findings. Due to the influence of the geometric boundary conditions, the spectrum could not be exactly matched to theory, specifically in the transition from an $f^1$ to an $f^0$ regime. Nevertheless, this research provides substantial evidence supporting the self-similar nature of turbulent flows within the inertial regime, and has implications for the broader application of the Zakharov-Kolmogorov spectrum to rotating shear flows.

The mental health crisis within the criminal justice system is a pressing concern with lengthy repercussions. Research indicates a substantial percentage of incarcerated individuals struggle with mental health issues, and upon release, they face an elevated risk of recidivism. This study aims to investigate the effects on mental health and criminal reentry of requiring therapy as a condition of probation. A randomized controlled trial was conducted with convicted offenders who were assigned either a required therapy group or a standard services group. The study's findings showed that participants in the required therapy group exhibited improved mental health outcomes, reduced substance abuse, and lower reincarceration rates compared to the standard services group. These results suggest that making therapy a condition of probation can have a positive impact on mental health, criminal reentry, and overall success in the community.

Medical image segmentation models are often developed using a combination of large amounts of unlabelled image data and a limited set of annotated images. For optimal performance, it is crucial that the model is properly initialized with the labelled data. Regrettably, common techniques such as data augmentation and generative models have limited success in enhancing model precision on a target dataset. A novel approach is presented here that utilizes a pre-trained model in a consistent manner, with the aim of determining whether it is possible to develop a straightforward yet effective method to enhance model precision on a target dataset. The proposed technique is examined and found to yield superior outcomes when compared to alternative methods. Code is openly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/zhengyang-wu/SSIS.

The ATLAS jet calorimeter trigger system will undergo a significant transformation for LHC's Phase-2, introducing a new, higher-speed front-end that must operate at a minimum speed of 640 MHz (from 80 MHz currently). This new design will utilize an advanced digital system to handle 1.4 Tebytes of information produced every second, necessitating a substantial boost in the system's input data rate. To manage this increased data rate, a novel, high-speed serial input circuit has been developed for the front-end by the CERN's ATLAS collaboration. Constructed with the use of Xilinx's UltraScale+ technology, this new circuit boasts twice the input data rate of the existing design. To test its performance, the circuit was prototyped and integrated into an ATLAS jet trigger demo board before being evaluated with the full ATLAS system at the CERN. The results showed that the circuit meets the requirements of the ATLAS jet calorimeter trigger system with a high level of reliability and accuracy.

The advancement of neural visual models has significantly improved the creation of realistic images, but generating accurate and dynamic images of humans from a text description remains a challenge. This study proposes a novel approach, articulating the model to include a skeleton or mesh to aid in image generation, which yields more precise and adaptable images of humans from text. We introduce VibeArt, a mesh-based model that transforms text descriptions into detailed, dynamic avatars and produces various styles of art. To prevent the model from getting stuck in local minima, we developed an innovative cycle-consistency algorithm using a conditionally generated background, which produces more accurate and versatile results. As evidenced by our experiments and user feedback, the proposed method excels in creating varied, dynamic, and racially inclusive avatars from diverse text descriptions.

Building on a cutting-edge graph neural network for quantum dynamics, we've developed a framework that provides transparent and interpretable results. We've demonstrated the effectiveness of this approach by using it to investigate and quantify the behavior of a system in question - specifically, an isolated atom experiencing strong laser light, a notoriously complex and chaotic phenomenon. Through application of a method called structured operator normalization, we've been able to ensure that the accuracy of our predictions is maintained even as we've incorporated an expert-designed structure that promotes meaningful connections and patterns in data. This approach has allowed us for the first time to make predictions about critical system variables that are based on more than just raw data - using graph attention units that are sensitive to the system's structural relationships. As a result, we've been able to identify the minimal set of essential interactions that are responsible for the system's behavior and make predictions about how other potential interactions would affect it. This has significant implications for applying machine learning models to other complex and high-stakes systems of all kinds.

The general method developed maximizes likelihood under constraints, leading to a legitimate solution for estimating the average parameter of a mixture of unknown component distributions, even if the mixture is not identifiable. A secondary application of the method yields an alternative approach for solving classical problems of estimating certain function parameters from a mixture of distributions.

Knowledge tracing has seen significant advancements through deep learning-based models, however the field lacks a comprehensive evaluation toolkit. To address this gap, we have developed pyKT, a thorough evaluation framework that encompasses various metrics, data preprocessing procedures, and a range of deep learning-based model implementations for knowledge tracing. This framework enables researchers to conduct methodological comparisons and model assessments by providing:
* A unifying structure for specifying evaluation protocols
* A collection of metrics that cover model performance, similarity, and relevance
* A suite of deep learning-based model implementations that have been optimally tuned for the AT-CBT dataset
* Detailed guidelines for designing and executing evaluation protocols
By offering pyKT, we aim to establish a common ground for evaluating deep learning-based knowledge tracing models and encourage the research community to build upon this framework.

Given a smooth variety $X$ that is not necessarily compact, we demonstrate that differential operators of elliptic type form a closed subspace within the topological vector space of differential forms, $\Omega(X)$. This outcome holds irrespective of $X$'s dimension. Notably, this conclusion does not follow from any prior findings related to the compactness of $X$.

Proofs in SMT solvers are generated dynamically and serve a dual purpose - not only are they crucial for verifying the validity of user assertions within the solver, they also facilitate the efficient reuse of previously derived proofs whenever similar assertions are re-circulated. Unfortunately, the versatility of these proofs remains severely limited due to the proprietary format employed by each respective solver. To break down these proof silos and promote greater proof portability, we introduce a novel format called Alethe, which combines elements from multiple sources, including SMT-LIB3 and TPTP, to create a more comprehensive proof structure. This extended proof structure is capable of expressing not only first-order logic proofs but also meta-theoretic properties and model contents, thereby enabling the seamless integration of multiple SMT solvers and reasoning systems. We have successfully demonstrated the efficacy of this format by successfully verifying a wide-ranging set of proofs with multiple SMT solvers, in addition to proving the soundness of this format with a separate verification tool.

Optimizing models across a network of participating devices through Federated Learning is a significant task, albeit hampered by the constraint that models can only be updated synchronously, which hinders performance. To circumvent this limitation, we incorporate a buffer to enable asynchronous accumulation of gradients within each device, unconstrained by synchronization requirements. This innovation allows the creation of optimized models that serve as inputs to a global optimizer, which is then communicated back to the participating devices. As a result, we derive an analytical framework to characterize the optimal solution and explore the theoretical benefits of this approach through a theoretical model. Our experiments demonstrate that our proposed framework yields improved performance in comparison to synchronous FL, particularly in scenarios with limited communication and where the network contains a diverse range of devices with varying computational capabilities.

For an improved automatic speech recognition system with limited labeled data, transfer learning is a widely used technique. Recent studies have shown that matching the embedding space of source and target languages can enhance performance. In this research, we propose a two-pronged approach to establish a target-language recognizer with the aid of a multilingual base model. Firstly, we draw upon data from diverse languages to train a rough set of models with low-target-language-labels, primarily relying on high-quality English labels. Secondly, we select models with high target-characteristics from the rough set and fine-tune them with a substantial amount of target-language data. Our method achieves a notable 12.8% reduction in target-language data requirements, surpassing prior art, and attains a 6.3% improvement in target-characteristic WER.

Graph neural network (GNN) research often relies on structured data represented as graphs, where nodes are embedded in a higher dimensional space to facilitate machine learning tasks. Despite significant advancements, comparing different node representation learning methods remains challenging due to a lack of standardized evaluation criteria. To address this disparity, our work introduces a novel evaluation framework that assesses the embeddings produced by GNNs, focusing on two key aspects: proximity preservation and structural role-based expertise. To support this framework, we've curated the Twitch Players dataset, comprising 10,072 nodes and 159 features, representing the online multiplayer gameplay of Twitch streamers. Our evaluation framework and accompanying dataset enable a more comprehensive comparison of GNNs, particularly in terms of their ability to capture expert roles within a structured context. Through our experiments, we demonstrate the efficacy of our evaluation framework and the valuable insights gained from the Twitch Players dataset in evaluating node representation learning methods.

The observation of a rhombus-shaped resonance at around $1500$ MeV in various $B$ meson decay channels to a pair of kaons has sparked intense discussion. Employing a dipole form factor that matches the $B$ meson form factor in a manner consistent with the Fubini-Stone theorem, we investigate the possibility of designating this resonance as the $\rho^0(1450)$. Through a comprehensive examination of existing data, our findings indicate that this resonance's characteristics are remarkably well-suited to its lower-mass counterpart, the $\rho^0(770)$. Moreover, we discover that the axial-vector contribution within the $K\KK$ system is minimal, thus primarily focusing on the contribution of the $\rho^0(1450)$ vector meson. Building upon this understanding, we explore the possibility of the $\rho^0(1450)$ being responsible for the $f_0(1500)$ and $f_J(1500)$ resonances observed in $B\to \pi(K)KK$ decays. This research was supported in part by the National Science Foundation (NSF) and the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee.

Researchers have previously suggested that a high-dimensional space with a negative cosmological constant may require a non-trivial "shadow dimension" to justify the standard form of the volume factor in its geometry. By extending the theory of high-dimensional spaces to include the concept of a shadow dimension, we find that it conforms to the principles of the Swampland program. Specifically, we find that the presence of a non-trivial shadow dimension satisfies the condition that the ratio of the vacuum energy to the volume of the space must be greater than a certain minimum value, and this satisfies the Swampland's "obstacle" constraint. Notably, we propose that the shadow dimension could take the form of a network of primordial black holes connecting different branches of the multiverse, and that it could constitute a significant fraction of the universe's matter density. If this is the case, we would expect to observe a distribution of primordial black holes with masses in the range of $\sim 10^{(-10))} M_{\odot}$ to $\sim 10^{7} M_{\odot}$.

A novel algorithm for regulating the force produced by a series elastic actuator has been developed. By combining a novel transmission force estimator and an advanced control algorithm, a highly precise level of force generation can be achieved. A key challenge in designing a elastic actuator is estimating the interaction force between the actuator and its environment, which is addressed by designing a novel transmission force estimator based on a nominal dynamic model of the actuator's transmission system. This estimator utilizes a unique measurement setup that enables the accurate calculation of a critical variable necessary for understanding the actuator's dynamics. A significant advantage of this estimator is its ability to handle complex nonlinear transmission systems by converting them into a linear state error calculator. To generate the optimal control signal necessary for precise force regulation, a nonlinear algorithm has been designed that utilizes the estimated transmission force and a novel reference frame, resulting in a system that can generate complex nonlinear forces with ease. To validate the effectiveness of this algorithm, a range of tests were conducted on a testbed featuring a highly complex nonlinear transmission system, demonstrating that it can generate extremely precise levels of force.

A flexible slab resting on a soft substrate is a fundamental configuration found in various settings, from human movements on pavement to the gait of walking animals and the locomotion of insects. Due to the significant impact that cracks within this system have on its overall functionality and efficiency, it is essential to develop a quantitative framework for calculating the critical stress at which these cracks form. By incorporating a broad range of experimental data, our research reveals that a crack will inevitably develop when the stress reaches approximately 1.9 times the shear modulus of the substrate, and this occurs before any notable failure in the system can occur. Interestingly, this finding suggests that the shear modulus of the substrate has a more substantial influence on crack formation than the friction between the slab and the substrate. Additionally, our research proposes that the most effective approach in preventing crack formation would be to lower the overall stress rather than modifying the properties of the system's components.

We investigate a range of SU(Nc) gauge theories involving three-dimensional scalar fields with multiple interacting terms in their potential. These interactions are fairly uniform across the various fields and can vary in their levels of coupling. When the coupling between different fields is minimal, our analysis reveals that a broad range of symmetry-breaking patterns can occur, potentially giving rise to Higgs states with significant mass. However, if the interaction between the fields is substantial, particularly in more closely coupled systems, we find that many of these symmetry-breaking patterns are hindered, leaving only a limited range of Higgs state mass possibilities. This occurs when the nature of the scalar potential prevails over the effects of the gauge group.

To enable marine robots to achieve cost-efficient and extensive underwater surveys, our approach introduces a novel method for modeling and utilizing temporal variation in sensor data based on Gaussian processes with sparsity. By incorporating temporal variation into the model, our method enhances prediction performance and cost optimization results. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through both theoretical calculations and real-world experiments.

We introduce Arrangement Networks, a novel architecture that efficiently
integrates feature transformations and a non-linear arrangement function using
a flexible, modular design. We demonstrate that this architecture offers
comparable performance to Nonlinear Block Transversal Networks and non-linear
transformer arrangements, while significantly reducing computational depth.
Furthermore, our analysis reveals that this architecture implicitly follows
multiple computation paths, enabling effective information fusion.

We investigate a static, spherically symmetric, and nonisotropic relativistic star consisting of a dual-fluid composite, made up of an ideal perfect fluid both within and outside of the star's boundary. By employing the conformal transformation method, we derive a set of GR equations that accurately capture the star's behavior and its surroundings. Through a series of confomal transformations, we ultimately arrive at a simplified set of Einstein Field Equation configurations that effectively model this dual-fluid scenario.

The distribution of spiral arms in a galaxy like the Milky Way remains a complex phenomenon that spiral arm models struggle to fully capture. While previous models have been developed to simulate spiral arms in a galaxy like the Milky Way, they often fall into one of two categories: dynamic models that simulate the galaxy's evolution and static models that reproduce observed arm features without considering the galaxy's dynamic history. In contrast, this study proposes a unique approach by integrating elements of both categories to create a more comprehensive model of a galaxy like the Milky Way. In this approach, the galaxy is divided into multiple segments, with each segment represented by a dynamic model that includes a rotating curve and a density profile, while also being subject to gravitational interactions from neighboring segments. A simple method was employed to dynamic models, using the Toomre Q-parameter to determine the presence of spiral arms. This method was effective in creating a galactic structure with spiral arms, and the results were validated by comparing them to observations of the Milky Way. Furthermore, this approach allows for the estimation of a galaxy's inclination angle and rotation curve using a method based on the maximum density of a galaxy along different radial paths. This study finds that the inclination angle of the Milky Way is approximately 20 degrees, while the rotation curve of a galaxy like the Milky Way can be accurately modeled using a linear function.

Galactic mergers significantly shape galaxy evolution, and doing so, mergers likely have a profound impact on galaxies residing in high-density environments. This current analysis focuses on a simulation of major mergers taking place within a fully developed galaxy cluster - a simulation performed with the use of a highly advanced supercomputer. A sophisticated modeling technique, incorporating the influence of magnetic fields on gas, allowed for an in-depth examination of how the magnetic field influences the amalgamation of two galaxies. Following the amalgamation, various properties of the newly formed galaxy were tracked over time. Unlike previous research, this analysis revealed that the presence of a magnetic field affects the structure of galaxy amalgamations in a more subtle manner than expected. However, a notable difference was observed in the behavior of gas and stars during the amalgamation. In the case of gas, a stronger magnetic field results in an increased resistance to the formation of a central black hole and an extended duration of hot, X-ray-emitting gas. Furthermore, a stronger magnetic field leads to an increased formation of molecular gas in the galaxy's central region, which in turn enhances the formation of a central black hole over time. In contrast, stars exhibit a decreased level of internal absorption and an increased scattering in a stronger magnetic field. In addition, a stronger magnetic field results in an increased presence of stars in the galaxy's central region.
