We demonstrate that introducing a controlled interaction between the qutrit and sound wave mode can effectively split a low-energy qutrit state into two non-overlapping states at higher energies. We also establish the accuracy of this method by calibrating the energy transfer using both theoretical modeling and experimental measurements. Furthermore, we find that the energy of the qutrit can be increased by a factor of up to 40 over its coupling with the photon field. We anticipate that this advancement will significantly enhance the simulation of sQED, enabling the exploration of qutrits in multiple degrees of freedom that are fundamental to this theory.

The interaction between a high-power laser and a thin polarized electron-positron vapor can create positrons, but their polarization relies on several factors, including positron generation mechanisms and the potential for polarization to be introduced during the formation of a vacuum gap. An alternative approach involves hitting a thin polarized metal foil with a high-power laser, as this produces a shock wave that accelerates electrons and results in the creation of a large number of positrons through vacuum radiation when the critical density is exceeded, potentially leading to positron polarization greater than 0.1%. Calculations indicate that if a 100 mJ 800 nm laser pulse is directed at a 5 micrometer thick gold foil with a density of 3.86 x 10^18 cm^-2 over an area of 1 square micrometers, a 2.5 x 10^8 Watts/cm^-2 intensity would produce a significant amount of positrons, with densities reaching as high as 10^9 cm^-2 and an average polarization exceeding 0.1%. However, this assumes that the positron polarization is solely the result of vacuum radiation when the critical density is exceeded and that there is no polarization introduced during the formation of a vacuum gap.

A group G is considered large if there exists an infinite number of distinct elements d, satisfying the condition that for every g in G, d*g equals the inverse of g. This condition essentially defines a large subgroup within G. We are particularly interested in the smallest number of elements required to describe an infinite number of large subgroups within a given finite group F. We refer to this smallest number as the algebraic diameter of F. In this study, we provide a comprehensive classification of all finite groups with an algebraic diameter equal to 3. We demonstrate that no non-abelian simple groups possess an algebraic diameter of 3. However, certain non-abelian simple groups can have an algebraic diameter of 2. We establish a connection between the algebraic diameter of a group and its subgroup structure, specifically focusing on the structure of its 2-local subgroups. We offer an open-ended problem related to the study of finite groups with an algebraic diameter of 3 or less. We prove that all finite groups with an algebraic diameter of 3 can be classified into one of the following categories: (1) a group whose 2-local subgroups consist of an odd number of Sylow 2-subgroups and is not isomorphic to a group within the family PS^3_{2n+1}, (2) a group whose 2-local subgroups consist of the maximum possible number of Sylow 2-subgroups and is not isomorphic to

A temperature sensor chip, capable of withstanding a wide voltage range from 0.6V to 1.8V, is proposed. It employs a novel temperature detection mechanism that utilizes a heavily doped region for temperature measurement. The sensor's temperature reading is obtained through a conversion formula based on the N-A and P-A current ratios. It achieves a precise temperature resolution of 0.24°C with an error of 1.4°C and consumes extremely low power of 1.06nJ per conversion cycle. Due to its minimal components and simple structure, the sensor is highly suitable for integrated system design.

Long-lasting stability in the magnetic fields of stars can be inferred by analyzing the small fluctuations in these fields. In this study, we've developed a rigorous framework for assessing the stability of magnetic fields in stars with symmetrical axes, specifically in p- and g-mode type fluctuations. This framework is applicable across various types of stellar magnetic fields, from non-degenerate stars to compact objects and magnetars. By integrating numerical solutions and semi-analytical models, we determined the conditions under which magnetic fields in stars can remain stable and consistent with observed values. These conditions include metrical field strength requirements, aligned with previous findings, as well as a requirement for the magnetic pressure equal to or greater than the surface gravity of the star. This new framework is a significant advancement in the study of magnetic fields in stars and will be an integral tool for future research in this field.

In this series of research papers, our primary objective is to develop a set of precise numerical methods for solving the equations derived from the functional renormalization group in fluid dynamics, particularly focusing on the FRG flow equations. To establish this, we first review renormalization group theory and then delve into the fundamentals of the FRG, its applications in physics, and relevant concepts. Next, we investigate the parametric space for zero-dimensional quantum field theories, exploring how the FRG captures the behavior of these theories and the role of symmetry in the renormalization group flow. Our testing framework is then used to assess the accuracy of our numerical methods for solving the FRG flow equations in both symmetric and asymmetric cases, taking into account various perturbations of the theory. Finally, we provide an overview of our computational strategy and the results obtained, which demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach for investigating the properties of zero-dimensional quantum field theories.

Music composition remains an intricate task for artificial intelligence models to grasp.
While successful in other text-based applications like translation and summarization, AI models flounder when attempting to create original music from a given theme or style through text descriptions.
This difficulty is compounded by the fact that describing music is fundamentally different from describing language, due to music's inherent melodic and harmonic components that cannot be easily captured in textual form.
To address this challenge, we introduce a novel approach, where an AI model is trained to generate music directly, bypassing the need for a textual interpretation of the given theme or style.
This approach, which we call meta-inquiry, allows the model to process the input music as a whole and produce an original composition with a probability distribution over various styles.
Our experiments demonstrate the efficacy of this method, resulting in a groundbreaking model that creates diverse, high-quality music in multiple styles.

Building on earlier work, we generalize key concepts from the field of Lie groupoids to smooth stacks. Specifically, we establish a theory of geometric objects that we term "Lie groupoid-like objects" or $\mathcal{LG}$-objects for short, which encompasses both Lie groupoids and Deligne-Mumford stacks equipped with a smooth structure. Within this framework, we define the notion of a morphism between such objects and investigate various properties of $\mathcal{LG}$-objects, including their relationship to algebraic equivalents and the presence of a natural topology. Furthermore, we establish connections to related constructs such as differentiable functor categories and Grothendieck topologies, and demonstrate that the stacks formed from $\mathcal{LG}$-objects share critical features with those from the traditional theory.

We present radio continuum observations of the young infrared dark cloud, Dragon, which suggests that there is a young massive protostar and protostar cluster forming within it. The radio continuum emissions from this region are found to be non-thermal in nature, indicating the presence of young massive stars and massive protostars that are actively engaging in the process of mass accumulation. Furthermore, observations of 1.3 mm continuum and 850 um submillimeter dust emissions provide key insights into the core and protostellar cluster's characteristics. The analysis of these emissions reveals that there is a distinct difference in the intensity of emissions towards the center of the cloud, suggesting the presence of a dense core with high mass accumulation rates. Models of thermal continuum emissions also support this finding, indicating that there are multiple low-mass protostars and a high-mass star or protostar with significant mass accumulation rates at the center of the cloud. The mass accumulation rates derived from these models are found to be in the range of 2-8 x 10^-5 Msol/yr for the low-mass protostars and 4-6 x 10^-4 Msol/yr for the high-mass star or protostar. The presence of a core with high mass accumulation rates within the Dragon cloud may indicate the early stages of massive star formation, making it a potential target for future observations.

Godel modal logic can be derived from Intuitionistic modal logic through the addition of the rule of double negation, leading to a similar relationship between Godel and Kleene algebras. Building on this connection, we introduce a family of relational structures that embody various extensions of Godel modal logic, including Heyting arithmetic with the double negation exclusion law and its counterpart, Baillargeon-Lemmon logic. These structures are essentially hybridizations of intuitionistic and classical modal relational structures. We then examine the equivalence between these relational structures and the associated Godel modal logic by establishing a correspondence with the algebraic frameworks comprising Godel and Kleene-Mouckoukette algebras. Furthermore, this correspondence allows us to demonstrate the representability of these logic systems through their respective structures and algebras.

LiDAR technology is widely utilized for gathering detailed point cloud data across various settings, including construction, and to accommodate growing security requirements, the collection of data is frequently performed around the clock. While numerous advanced methods have been developed to automate processing of such data, especially for detecting and blocking hazards on roads, many existing techniques are primarily designed for use on systems from the same manufacturer. A unique approach has been presented that leverages deep learning to extract relevant information from LiDAR point clouds, enabling the detection of obstacles across multiple domains without the need for explicit scanning. In addition, this approach enables continuous data collection without posing additional workload on surveyors. A key innovation of this method is the development of a novel 3D metric learning framework that enables direct comparison of LiDAR point clouds. To validate this approach, it was tested on three diverse datasets in outdoor settings, and the results show its effectiveness and efficiency. The code and models for this project have been made publicly accessible.

By categorizing a broad class of random field models that incorporate stochastic processes and determine their second moment properties on the sphere, researchers have established standard formulas for computing mean and variance. This work specifically explores a subcategory of models dubbed IID$\mathcal{X}$, where the stochastic process is divided into separate components located at each point on the sphere. The key finding for the variance of a function of the field is derived, employing a novel recurrence formula that significantly improves the existing method's complexity. The new algorithm has a $O(n\log n)$ time complexity, a substantial improvement over the previous $O(n^2)$ time complexity. To validate the new algorithm, a comparison with an alternative method has been made, showing a notable increase in processing speed. The proposed algorithm has been implemented and its efficiency verified.

The search for high-energy cosmic neutrinos and ultra-high-energy cosmic particles has been ongoing for many years, with missions like IceCube and the Pierre Auger Observatory working tirelessly to understand these enigmatic phenomena. Combining their extensive datasets offers valuable insights, potentially revealing the sources and spatial relationships of these particles. By correlating neutrino and UHECR arrival directions with each other and with various landmarks in the sky, such as active galactic nuclei, galaxy clusters, and the Great Attractor, we employed a statistical test to examine the presence of excess neutrino or UHECR events around these features. Our findings show that UHECR events are disproportionately concentrated towards the galactic center and nearby, whereas cosmic neutrinos exhibit a random distribution. Furthermore, we observed UHECR excesses directionally connected to several AGN and galaxy clusters but found no such connection with neutrinos.

The interaction between a liquid surface and a solid object is influenced by several factors including surface tension, viscosity, and the nature of the surface. Research has been conducted to study the influence of a rough surface on different types of liquids, revealing a distinct category known as stick-slip phenomena. This study is aimed at investigating the effect of a rough surface on a specific type of liquid, namely a foam, which is composed of mobile bubbles. Previous research has demonstrated that the normal force and stick-slip behavior of a foam are directly proportional to the viscosity of the liquid, suggesting that the property responsible for this behavior is the foam's own resistance rather than that of the underlying liquid. In order to further explore this aspect, the study measures the force and stick-slip behavior of a foam subjected to a rough surface at various levels of stress and temperature. The results indicate that neither an increase in stress nor a decrease in temperature has a significant impact on the force or stick-slip behavior. Furthermore, it was observed that the normal force and stick-slip behavior are directly proportional to the temperature, in contrast to the inverse relationship found in other liquids. This discrepancy is attributed to the thermal expansion of the bubbles within the foam, which alters its mechanical properties. In addition, the research demonstrates that the coefficient of friction remains constant and is solely a function of the texture and temperature but not stress or other variables. This unique thermal expansion of the foam's coefficient of friction is believed to originate from the restricted thermal expansion of

The challenge of developing effective and precise cancer diagnosis lies in the fact that primary tumors have a low mortality rate and often metastasize in a relatively late stage, making it crucial to detect and diagnose skin lesions in an early and accurate manner. In this study, a novel approach was developed for identifying malignant skin carcinomas from a diverse range of lesions, incorporating a combination of features extracted via deep learning and the calculation of probabilistic outlier detection to identify and exclude anomalous lesions extracted from the ISIC 2018 dataset. This approach was demonstrated to achieve a high accuracy of 94.59% in distinguishing between benign and malignant lesions. A comparison with existing models revealed that this approach yields superior performance, exceeding the current state-of-the-art models in accuracy.

The theory of finger growth in a Hele-Shaw cell is often used to model viscous finger formation in various situations. However, research has shown that certain factors can cause a deviation from the predicted pinching of the finger. While some of these factors lead to a curved finger shape, others result in a non-compact finger. Some possible explanations include the presence of surface tension, a rotating plate, or differences in fluid density. In this study, we investigate how these factors influence finger growth in a Hele-Shaw cell with a significant impact, particularly when the imposed stress is irregular. Our findings indicate that both surface tension and the factors affecting stress distribution can lead to a curved finger shape. Additionally, we have identified a stress discontinuity as the cause of non-compact finger behavior. Furthermore, our research demonstrates that normal-mode analysis can be used to explain the behavior of the Hele-Shaw cell when the imposed stress is regular.

One of the fundamental issues in simulating classical mechanical systems using artificial neural networks is the problem of varying phase space volume. Our research introduces an innovative solution to this challenge by proposing the use of Hamiltonian paths in place of constant energy simulations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to the expansion of an ideal gas, obtaining accurate results that surpass previous methods.

Scientists have identified various ethynyl derivatives of aromatic and cycloaliphatic compounds in interstellar space, primarily through the detection of cyano and dihydrogen derivatives. This study focuses on cyclopentadiene and benzene to determine the abundance of their ethynyl forms and the formation pathways of the cyano and hydrogen variants. Column densities of the cyclopentadiene and benzene derivatives have been calculated from existing observations, with estimates indicating that the ethynyl, cyano, and dihydrogen forms of these molecules have similar abundance patterns. This study also reports the first detection of two isomeric forms of ethynyl cyclopentadiene, at frequencies corresponding to rest wavelengths of 1.677 and 1.683 millimeters, with a rotational temperature of approximately 4 K. Models predicting the formation of these compounds suggest that they share a common precursor and could be differently complexed with a metal ion such as Fe^+ or Mg^+, with varying ring slippage. This interpretation is supported by computational modeling, which indicates that the two isomeric forms can coexist and have similar energies. The relative abundance of the ethynyl, cyano, and dihydrogen derivatives of these molecules is found to be in the ratio of approximately 1:2:10, with an overall abundance in TMC-1 significantly lower than in the Galaxy.

The current attention-based neural machine translation paradigm significantly excels previous methods but still has a crucial limitation: the attention mechanism is only computed based on historical context, which can lead to translation errors due to a lack of consideration for future context, including the target sentence. To overcome this restriction, we propose a novel look-forward attention mechanism that allows the source sentence to gaze at the target sentence's past, current, or anticipated language within the sentence. Moreover, we suggest a way for the attention mechanism to focus on either the source or the target sentence unidirectionally or bidirectionally. Experimental evaluations on WMT14 En-Fr, WMT15 De-En, and WMT16 En-De demonstrate notable improvements in BLEU scores resulting from the proposed look-forward attention mechanism.

The concept of computational paradigms has been introduced, categorizing grid computing as one of several models. This paper questions the validity of this classification and investigates whether grid computing was inaccurately defined due to a translation error. It presents a possible explanation for this misdefinition, drawing from the experiences of the author, Fred Berman, and offers a revised classification of computational paradigms.

We introduce a novel cosmological model that incorporates a dark fluid with both dissipation and expansion properties in a complex and dynamic universe. This model's structure differs significantly from standard dark energy models, which typically involve a simple exponential expansion. Instead, our model's expansion follows a more intricate path, shaped by a nonlinear equation influenced by a dissipation coefficient. This coefficient, in turn, is affected by a gravitational force in a complex feedback loop. As a result, the model's behavior cannot be accurately captured using a linear perturbation approach. Our analysis focuses on a specific non-linear scenario, but the model's fundamental characteristics can be applied to other non-linear contexts. Building on our research, it would be interesting to explore more complex scenarios and determine the model's predictive capabilities in relation to existing cosmological data.

Students' curiosity plays a significant role in their motivation to learn, yet little research explores how it evolves throughout a lesson or if it can be stimulated through different teaching methods. This study examines the effects of an innovative, multi-faceted instructional approach on the development of curiosity in small groups of students as they engage in science activities. The approach combines problem-centered learning with emotional support and involves two facilitators who provide both instructional and social support. Curiosity in these groups is measured through self-assessment, observation, and analysis of think-aloud reflections. The study consists of 20 groups of 3-4 students, with each group receiving 30 minutes of instruction. The results reveal that this approach significantly boosts curiosity levels, with most students exhibiting elevated curiosity throughout the lesson. Interestingly, students with initially low curiosity showed the greatest increase in curiosity. A notable number of students exhibited a non-linear curiosity trajectory, with curiosity levels dropping initially before rebounding in the latter half of the lesson. This study suggests that an approach combining rigorous intellectual challenges and emotional support can effectively stimulate curiosity in small groups of students. However, the non-linear curiosity trajectory observed in some students highlights the complex and dynamic nature of curiosity, suggesting that future research should explore various factors contributing to this phenomenon, including individual differences, prior knowledge, and the interplay between different aspects of the instructional approach.

This research introduces a novel parametric family of Gaussian random field models, centered on the Mat\'ern formula, that can be applied to any graph and a range of kernel functions. By characterizing the hyperparameter in terms of the graph's properties and establishing connections to random walk and graph Laplacian techniques, our approach extends and generalizes previous models such as the Gaussian Random Field and Lasso-Lama. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through multiple synthetic and real-world experiments, showing it achieves a better balance between model complexity and fit.

The growing popularity of mobility sharing services has generated substantial amounts of data that can be utilized for detecting and monitoring urban infrastructure, ultimately contributing to the maintenance and development of intelligent, data-driven transportation systems. Despite the potential of these services, the optimal detection of roads through vehicle navigation remains an unexplored area, especially in areas with dense tree cover where existing methods fall short. This paper investigates the optimal detection of urban roads utilizing ridesharing vehicle navigation data, particularly focusing on systems featuring a large number of continuously moving vehicles with limited navigation updates. We employ a stochastic process to model the detection process and develop a mathematical framework to maximize the expected detection rate of roads, ultimately reducing to a problem of determining optimal sensing intervals. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through simulations and a real-world experimentation setup, finding that our proposed strategy outperforms existing methods and yields substantial increases in detection rates in scenarios with limited vehicle navigation.

Researchers are working to understand why the cosmos contains so few antielectrons, despite expectations from certain theories, such as those involving dark matter or extra sterile neutrino populations. The availability of more precise data from experiments like the Belle II or a future LHCb upgrade could either confirm certain theories or rule out others, potentially including those related to dark matter or extra neutrino populations. Until then, these models will remain speculative and could distort our interpretation of cosmic phenomena. For instance, models involving dark energy may be validated through cosmic observations, but models involving neutrino dark energy will require direct access to neutrino properties. The likelihood of certain models being valid will be influenced by experimental outcomes from experiments like the Belle II or a future LHCb upgrade, particularly when studying rare processes such as the decay of a charmonium particle into an antielectron and invisible particles. The significance of these experiments will be determined by the available data, but even a relatively small number of observed events could provide significant evidence for certain models, while a much larger number would be required to confirm others.

Previous research introduced a new method called SDIMSIM for system differential equations, incorporating variable stepsize options. This study builds upon that work by fine-tuning the method for use on non-stiff problems, specifically obtaining an order of two when employing constant step sizes and successfully adapting the method to work with variable step sizes. Numerical experiments are also conducted to demonstrate the method's effectiveness.

This work introduces the multivariate functional singular spectrum examination (MFSSX) technique, enabling analysis of functional data in two-dimensional space. Building upon the singular spectrum analysis (SSA) method, MFSSX offers a comprehensive approach for combining and comparing data sets, even those with different temporal and spatial dimensions. In our research, we apply this method to investigate temperature patterns in the Northern Hemisphere during the 20th century, using a vast dataset consisting of 37 globally dispersed locations. With a focus on the Atlantic European region, our results reveal a distinct pattern of temperature variability in this area, showing a notable 50-year cycle and a more recent temperature increase. When expanding the analysis to a broader geographical scope, the pattern holds for the European and Asian regions but only exhibits a 50-year cycle in Asia. Notably, temperature trends in the Americas and Africa do not align with these patterns. Furthermore, our research highlights the significance of considering the Atlantic Multidecadal Oscillation (AMO) in temperature modeling. With the AMO's influence factored in, the temperature trends in the Northern Hemisphere regions become more coherent, mirroring global temperature trends. Conversely, the AMO's impact is itself affected by global temperature trends, as observed through the lens of MFSSX.

Deep learning-based automated driving systems rely on video input and are trained end-to-end, but their responsiveness and stability are called into question due to the ease with which they can be tricked into making sudden sharp turns. Our research reveals that these systems are both overresponsive to certain stimuli and prone to oscillating between normal and excessive steering actions. We demonstrate the existence of steering attractors, where minor variations in input video lead to substantial deviations in output steering, and show that defense against attacks can be achieved by incorporating a control policy into the training process, either through an additional control-based loss function or by training the system to minimize the distance between its predicted steering and a reference path. We also explore additional techniques, including non-saturating output activation, global response normalization, and incorporating a fake future state into the self-driving system's prediction pipeline, and find that these methods provide some level of protection against attacks.

This study examines a one-dimensional random walk that continues until a specific time interval is reached, and our main objective is to analyze the long-term behavior of the probability of which side the walk is on, given that it has been walking for a substantial amount of time. We have established that regardless of the distribution of steps, the probability will converge to an asymmetric probability distribution, where the walk is more likely to be on one side than the other. We further found that the higher the mean number of steps taken, the greater the difference in probabilities will be, and we provide an intuitive explanation for this phenomenon. Notably, our results apply to a wide range of step distributions, including both discrete and continuous distributions.

The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate key aspects of plasma-edge interactions under ITER-like conditions. IShTAR features a large, 12-meter long, tongue-shaped plasma chamber with an area of 1.2 square meters where a high-density plasma is created by an 80 kW helicon plasma generator operating in the 13.56 MHz frequency range. Due to the limited accessibility of the plasma inside the chamber, remote diagnosis of the plasma is essential for maintaining optimal generator performance and ensuring reliable operation. This contribution focuses on the spectroscopic analysis of the helicon-generated plasma using a sophisticated diagnostic system that incorporates multiple plasma diagnostics, including a Langmuir probe, an energy analyzer, a Thomson spectrometer, and an echellette spectrometer. By examining plasma parameters such as density, electron temperature, and flow velocity, the study confirms that the helicon generator produces a steady and consistent plasma state in the helicon mode of operation.

This research paper presents a mathematical model to analyze the dynamics of a biological control model that features a pathogen as the controlling agent. The model incorporates the impact of environmental factors on the efficacy of the pathogen, specifically the reduction of its own life cycle and the life cycle of the target organism it aims to control. The model is based on a system of ordinary differential equations and is analyzed through the construction of a Lyapunov function to determine its equilibrium points and stability. The model's equilibrium points are found to be asymptotically stable, and a theorem is established to validate this stability under minimal and non-minimal disruption conditions. A numerical study is also conducted to examine the model's behavior and test the results of the theoretical analysis. The model's applications and its potential to be developed into a more complex model are discussed in the context of microbial pest control.

This study presents a novel approach, W-Net, for automatically identifying and precisely outlining individual cell nuclei within histopathological images. We have demonstrated the effectiveness of this method by applying it to a dataset containing 6000 annotated nuclei, which resulted in a precision of 88.6%, a recall of 87.7%, and a AUC-ROC of 97.14% in testing. Our approach has been successfully integrated into a system for detecting invasive regions within images of prostate tissue. Notably, this system has achieved a higher detection accuracy than medical specialists in 9 out of 11 cases. The code associated with this study has been made publicly accessible.

The converse of Hilbert's theorem 90 has been a significant concern in noncommutative class field theory. It can be expressed as the equivalence between two statements: on one hand, having a commutative torsion theory that allows for the extension of idempotents; on the other hand, being able to localize global function fields in a specific way. This paper focuses on the case of function fields of genus zero and establishes the condition that for a specific group of Galois extensions (namely the symplectic and odd special orthogonal groups) to have a connection with the idempotents, it is sufficient to localized in a local field of characteristic two. This result did not hold in other local fields of positive characteristic.

A graph G is considered detectable N times, denoted as G being in D^N, if its hamiltonian route index can be determined N times. In this study, we examine whether an iterated line graph under the D^N set of graphs maintains the property of having a determinable hamiltonian route index when N is 2 or greater. If not, we aim to identify a specific N value at which the property is broken.

This research develops a solitary-cell mathematical model to analyze the pyroptotic cell death induced by SARS-CoV-2 and the effects of anti-inflammatory responses on the virus's infection cycle. Pyroptosis, a form of programmed cell death characterized by the rupture of the cell membrane, plays a crucial role in combating infections by releasing pro-inflammatory cytokines and killing the invading pathogen. However, an overactive inflammatory response can also contribute to the destruction of healthy cells, impeding the recovery of patients. Building on existing research, our model integrates stochastic events, pH oscillations, and the complex interactions between the host and the virus. It provides a framework for examining how anti-inflammatory interventions, such as the release of IL-4, influence the infection dynamics and cell death induction. Through numerical simulations, our model investigates the impact of IL-4 on the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, cell death, and the persistence of the virus. These findings suggest that IL-4 can reduce cell death, the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines, and the persistence of the virus, highlighting the intricate balance between host defense and the need to prevent excessive inflammation during SARS-CoV-2 infection.

External influences such as temperature, light, and sound can hinder robots' ability to perform tasks through learning. This paper introduces a groundbreaking approach to automatically identify and eliminate external factors that affect state and reward information in reinforcement learning tasks. This breakthrough enables the efficient training of robots in complex, real-world environments by allowing them to focus on internal state and reward information that is not affected by external noise. This approach is highly versatile, applicable to various reinforcement learning algorithms and state representations. Moreover, this paper showcases the significant performance enhancements it provides, showcasing a notable improvement of 157% in success rate when using the new method.

A blockchain-based smart contract on Tezos, dubbed a smart contract, is validated on the network through a proof-of-stake process that relies on the contributions of bakers who verify and vote on contracts before they are deployed. Given the importance of a thorough examination prior to voting, bakers need efficient and reliable methods to assess contracts accurately. To address this requirement, we present HELMHOLTZ, a cutting-edge validation tool developed specifically for Tezos contracts, leveraging the refinements module of the Coq proof assistant to ensure the accuracy and safety of contracts before they are deployed to the Tezos network. By integrating refinements with the Idris programming language, we demonstrate the feasibility of complex contract validation, and to showcase its capabilities, we provide a practical example of a validated contract from a real-world application.

In recent years, graph convolutional neural networks (GCNNs) have gained significant popularity due to their ability to effectively operate on graph-structured data without the need for converting data into a fixed Euclidean space. Nevertheless, a crucial aspect of GCNNs, the convolutional process, remains poorly understood. Our research aims to illuminate the mysteries surrounding this process by comparing it to the matched filtering method in signal processing, thereby providing a comprehensive and intuitive explanation of how GCNNs work. Through this analogy, we demonstrate that the use of the Aggregated Attention (AG) graph attention layer leads to a maximum likelihood estimator, resulting in a filter function that combines the characteristics of a traditional filtering function and an attention mechanism. Our complementary study introduces an alternative to the AG layer, resulting in a filter function that emulates that of GCNNs. This achievement highlights the vast potential for applying matched filtering methods in topological deep learning frameworks.

By modifying the Einstein-Hilbert action with the addition of a scalar field coupled to gravity via a topological Chern-Simons term, the properties of general relativity are altered to accommodate non-trivial scalar field configurations that may arise in response to boundary conditions. This revised theory successfully models rotating black holes and solitons, even in the presence of gauge forces, and facilitates a clear understanding of how a non-trivial scalar field develops in response to boundary conditions imposed at infinity. Furthermore, it enables the precise calculation of the scalar field's amplitude as a function of the angular momentum or soliton mass, enabling a distinction between solitons and certain types of black holes that was previously impractical.

We've discovered a novel class of integrable systems on the sphere, characterized by reversible and irreversible symmetries. This finding extends the well-known integrable systems on the sphere, which are based on reversible symmetries alone. A key aspect of our discovery is the explanation of non-reversible symmetries through the use of "w-matrices," a concept initially explored in the context of the Yang-Baxter equation. Our work also establishes a link between our integrable systems and a well-studied set of quantum Hamiltonians, ensuring their equivalence when the systems are mapped from sphere geometry to hyperbolic geometry. Furthermore, we've identified a connection between our integrable systems and quantum group reductions of the Yang-Baxter equation, leading to further potential applications and future research directions.

This paper presents a novel approach to enhance the accuracy of ultrasound elastography by correcting lateral displacement estimation.  A key source of error in elastography is the inexact calculation of tissue displacement, primarily resulting from the imprecise location of the virtual source in synthetic aperture ultrasound imaging. To address this issue, this research proposes a new method, Virtual Origin Synthetic Aperture (VOSA), which involves determining the exact position of the virtual source in synthetic aperture imaging. The VOSA method was experimentally tested on a phantom and compared to the conventional synthetic aperture imaging technique. Results showed a notable improvement in the error of displacement estimation, indicating that VOSA is a more precise method. Although slightly slower than conventional synthetic aperture imaging, VOSA offers significant advantages in elastography. Therefore, it is suitable for a variety of elastography applications requiring precise lateral displacement estimation.

Students learn programming best through hands-on coding, but they also need to understand algorithms and flow of programs. To bridge this gap, a secondary benefit is achieved - preparing students for success in careers where automated tools are used. However, writing code is not the only way for students to understand algorithms; a new method is proposed that allows algorithms to be explained using pseudocode containing variables of different types and control structures. This approach is shown to be effective by presenting an online platform and a related educational approach that's being tested in a classroom setting.

The concept of Ramsey character was initially introduced by Tomás Kalás in 2005 as a measure to evaluate Ramsey numbers within the Boolean algebras defined by a set of posets. This paper builds upon the work of F. M. Jackson, F. Yang, and F. Zamora in 2019 by determining the exact values or infinite sets for the Ramsey character $\lambda_P(N)$ for a vast array of $V$-shaped posets $P$.

In the context of information retrieval, where we have a dataset of $n$ points in $d$ dimensions and a target parameter $k$, a significant challenge lies in identifying a subset of $k$ centers that can effectively group the remaining data efficiently. The standard $k$-means clustering algorithm achieves optimal results but suffers from a substantial computational cost, making it impractical for large-scale data sets. In contrast, a range of dynamic algorithms has been developed to strike a balance between performance and efficiency, with most existing analyses focusing on results in lower-dimensional spaces or with specific structural characteristics. In this paper, we introduce a new, simple and efficient dynamic $k$-means algorithm based on random sampling, which produces a center subset that can group the data in $O(nt)$ time, with a significant reduction in computational cost compared to traditional methods. We establish a non-uniform upper bound on the covering ratio of the data with a factor of $O(k^{3/2})$, which is close to the best known lower bound for at least two times the target size. This upper bound applies to any data set with a unique structure and holds a general form, with a value of $O(k^{3/2})$ covering the special cases of data sets with specific structures. We introduce the concept of a circular probability as the minimum requirement for n+1 equiprobable and mutually exclusive options to display n levels of nontransitive behavior. Circular probabilities exceed the threshold of 1 when n is two or greater. A set of circumstances that achieves the minimum requirement for nontransitivity is referred to as optimal. Optimal circumstances always involve an arrangement in which one option consistently beats the one preceding it, leading to a pattern that repeats every time the sequence is cycled through all its variations. This pattern guarantees the existence of an arrangement that exhibits nontransitive properties for any number of elements, making it inherently different from sequences requiring a specific ordering to produce nontransitive results.

Recently, deep learning techniques have gained popularity for enhancing low-dose CT images, particularly through unsupervised denoising using CycleGAN, due to their ability to produce high-quality images without requiring paired training data. However, existing methods have several limitations: they often involve complicated multi-stage training and may not effectively capture the unique contrast characteristics of low-dose CT images. In this study, we introduce a novel unsupervised cycleGAN framework, where a separate adaptation network is employed to align the cycle-consistency loss, but only switches its application during training through an AdaIN connection. By simplifying the training process and introducing contrast-preserving constraints, our model exhibits superior denoising performance, according to evaluation metrics, including the PSNR, SSIM, and FANET scores, and outperforms state-of-the-art deep learning models in multiple assessments.

Recent contrastive pre-training methods have achieved significant success in dialogue comprehension, despite being limited by the expense of gathering parallel dialogue data. To address this challenge, we introduce SPACE-2, a tree-structured semi-supervised contrastive pre-training framework for dialogue comprehension. Based on structural semantic models, SPACE-2 incorporates both structural and sequential information to represent dialogue semantics. To reduce data requirements, SPACE-2 utilizes a flexible annotation strategy that leverages existing labeled data for limited additional annotation. The model is then trained via a semi-supervised contrastive learning framework to refine dialogue representations and learn supplementary information. Experimental evaluations show that SPACE-2 achieves superior performance on dialogue understanding and few-shot learning tasks, surpassing other baselines by a margin of 2.1% on average.

This research confirms that an ideal fluid spacetime with an expanding and contracting cosmological constant harbors a soliton that is linked to a specific manifold configuration - namely, a manifold with a conformally Skew-symmetric Ricci-Yamabe metric. We further establish that a conformally lambda(Y)-harmonic soliton is equivalent to a conformally lambda(Y)-Einstein soliton, and we provide a theoretical proof. We also demonstrate that a conformally lambda(Y)-Einstein soliton can be simplified to a lambda(Y)-Einstein soliton when the fluid's pressure and the cosmological constant display specific relationships. Building on these findings, we prove that a lambda(Y)-Einstein soliton can be simplified to a lambda(E)-Einstein soliton when the fluid's pressure and the cosmological constant adhere to specific relationship, which can be further simplified to a condition where the Ricci operator acts on the Weyling tensor in a harmonic manner on the ideal fluid spacetime.

To study the rotational characteristics of distorted halo nuclei, we employed the angular momentum projection method onto wave functions derived from the deformed relativistic Hartree-Bogoliubov theory in continuum. Using this approach, we investigated rotational states in isotopes of $^{32}$Mg, $^{40}$Mg, and $^{42}$Mg, specifically examining how distortions in the halo shape influence rotational excitations. Our findings indicate that shape uncoupling effects play a crucial role in distorted halo nuclei, and they cannot be neglected. Furthermore, we found that the amplitude of intrinsic wave functions plays a significant part in determining rotational characteristics.

A common approach in video super-resolution is the recurrent structure, with the BasicVSR method being one of the top-performing frameworks, leveraging bidirectional propagation and feature alignment to utilize information from the input video. In our research, we upgrade BasicVSR by integrating guided propagation and a deformable alignment technique to more effectively exploit temporal information, primarily employing the hourglass transformer for feature extraction and aggregation. We also introduce a simple yet effective way to enhance training efficiency and generalize the method to video interpolation. Our experiments demonstrate that the upgraded model achieves superior performance and versatility across SR and interpolation tasks.

Due to the intense radiation in heavy-ion collisions, the LHeC can offer a substantial increase in luminosity, allowing for more precise investigation of proton-proton collisions, specifically at muon colliders running at the TeV level, where vector boson production serves a crucial role. Despite significant advances, current proton-proton colliders lack the necessary precision to fully understand the properties of vector bosons, particularly in high-energy environments. The muon colliders offer unique advantages, such as intrinsely low radiation backgrounds and the ability to measure the rapidity distribution of final states, enabling more precise vector boson mass measurements through overlapping proton bunches, with an expected level of 0.1 GeV in 10% of the mass range. Furthermore, combining the production of W and Z bosons permits self-calibration of luminosity at different energy levels, allowing for a more accurate determination of vector boson production rates. Ultimately, this will lead to a more precise understanding of the proton-proton interaction and the properties of vector bosons.

In a reinforcement learning environment with multiple tasks, model-based multi-task reinforcement learning models are often vulnerable to a significant performance decline when introduced to new tasks that are not closely related to previously learned tasks. This performance drop is attributed to the inherent property of negative correlation between the predictions of different tasks. To circumvent this issue, we propose an innovative modular prediction architecture that exploits the unique distribution of each task's state visits to prevent the destructive interference of task predictions. By applying this architecture to a range of multi-task reinforcement learning scenarios with disparate task distributions, we demonstrate a substantial improvement over current state-of-the-art methods.

This research paper focuses on approximating solutions to a specific type of parabolic equation using a specific type of degenerate parabolic equation in a noncompact metric space with a compact boundary. We first establish the convergence of the approximations to the solutions of the parabolic equation as the approximations become more precise. We then derive a rate at which the approximations converge to the solutions of the parabolic equation. This result is achieved under the condition that the solutions of the parabolic equation possess a certain level of smoothness. We also discuss the validity of our results in a more general setting.

Kurt Godel, along with colleagues Alonzo Church, Stephen Kleene, and Rosser, first discussed the concept of a universal theorem in 1930. Not long after, Godel, in his famous 1930 lecture, referred to the potential for a universal theorem to be used in a diagonalization argument. In 1931, Godel published his famous incompleteness theorems, and the following year Church proved the existence of a universal theorem. In the early 1930s, Kleene and Rosser developed methods for constructing models that avoided the possibility of a universal true sentence existing, achieving this by essentially 'killing' any universal sentence through their construction. This work predates the development of computability theory and Kripke's schema, and demonstrates that a significant portion of the intuitive basis for the incompleteness theorems can be derived solely from the properties of computability.

This paper formulates the three spheres theorem for functions solving a complex analytic transport equation, essentially an adaptation of the Bochner's theorem from harmonic analysis. In particular, we establish the theorem using a method based on a modified sub-Laplacian operator and subsequent application of a result by Frenkel and Ruppert.

When conducting field studies, researchers often encounter situations where collecting data from an entire population is impractical due to limited access. In such cases, they may need to gather information from a subset of the population in a specific geographic area. When the population is not stationary and difficult to enumerate, researchers must often rely on a method where they travel from one location to another, selectively approaching potential subjects to participate in the study. This paper proposes a new sequence-based method for sampling that takes into consideration both geographical balance and the sequence in which potential subjects are approached. Unlike existing methods that prioritize either geographical balance or efficiency, this method enables researchers to collect data while achieving a level of geographical balance without excessive waste of precious sampling opportunities. Through simulated data and real-world applications, our method demonstrates substantial improvements over existing approaches.

In robotics, adjusting an end-mounted camera to match the orientation of an object is a challenging problem that has not yet been fully resolved. Current methods can often locate object features but struggle to accurately determine the camera's optimal orientation. A novel approach has been proposed that leverages machine learning to tackle this issue using only one image per object. The method first identifies key features, establishes point-to-point correspondences, and then employs a deep learning network to refine the camera's orientation. Comprehensive tests conducted with a variety of objects demonstrate that this method can effectively find the optimal camera orientation with a high degree of accuracy.

In fields like physics and engineering, solving an inverse problem - determining the underlying cause from the effects - is a common challenge. It involves deriving a unknown process that generated observable outcomes. We frame this as a problem of extracting a random variable's posterior distribution given its associated features, which we achieve by proposing a novel approach to approximately sample from this distribution. Our method is a regulated conditional Generative Adversarial Network that requires minimal prior knowledge and ensures the generated outcomes match the statistical characteristics of the observed data. We apply and evaluate our approach through numerical experiments and a real-world analysis of medical diagnosis. Results show that our method outperforms alternative techniques.

This article examines the concept of invariant surfaces in dynamical systems from a mathematical perspective. Specifically, it explores and generalizes the approach used in previous studies, applying it to a broader category of dynamical systems that incorporate fractional derivatives. The article particularly focuses on investigating the presence of invariant surfaces in these dynamical systems, employing a novel method that leverages properties of the Caputo fractional derivative. Key findings indicate that certain dynamical systems featuring nonlocal capabilities do not possess invariant surfaces near certain equilibrium points, providing a more comprehensive understanding in the context of fractional dynamical systems. The article also offers a comparison with related works and a discussion on potential applications and related problems.

Due to the limited coverage of THz communication's line-of-sight range, beam training is crucial for establishing high-quality connections in this frequency band. However, the time-consuming nature of traditional beam training techniques can conflict with the transient nature of indoor applications, where users are constantly moving and creating new channel conditions. In response, we propose an adaptive, learning-based approach that efficiently updates beam information over time. By leveraging reinforcement learning to update and refine the optimal beam in response to changing channel conditions, this approach can significantly reduce the time required for beam formation and improve the overall performance of the system. In our analysis, we develop a mathematical model of the proposed system and simulate various scenarios to demonstrate the advantages of our method. Notably, our results show that the new approach can achieve data transfer rates up to 10 times faster and reduce errors by 90% under certain conditions.

The interstellar medium is home to numerous structures that impact the propagation of radio waves and other forms of electromagnetic radiation. By analyzing the variations in brightness of pulsar signals as they travel through the interstellar medium, researchers can gain insights into the composition and dynamics of the medium. This study focuses on the interstellar medium surrounding the pulsar B1133+16 by examining changes in brightness of the pulsar's signal over an 11-year period. Although the data shows little change, it is not sensitive enough to detect the smaller structures that are typically associated with the pulsar's radio arc. The study suggests that a significant aspect of the medium, spanning approximately 3.6 parsecs, is relatively smooth and uniform, with an average density of 0.83 electrons per cubic centimeter. Furthermore, the study indicates that the line of sight to the pulsar is about 5.3 parsecs from the edge of the radio arc and that the medium is being drained at a rate of 12.5 kilometers per second.

This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-sensitive dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using an autoregressive probabilistic framework, but its lack of explicit pitch processing leads to inconsistent pitch output. To address this, QPNet embeds pitch information within dilated convolution's stride and depth parameters, allowing for the spontaneous emergence of a pitch contour during audio synthesis. In QPNet, a separate encoder extracts and conveys pitch information from input waveforms to multiple sub-networks with distinct pitch sensitivities. The learned pitch contours modulate the convolutional stride and depth of these sub-networks, effectively processing long-duration information and expanding the model's expressiveness. Experimental evaluations demonstrate improved pitch control, higher quality audio generation, and superior model training stability compared to the standard WN.

The objective of this research is to introduce MADARi, a novel online tool developed to simultaneously mark up Arabic texts morphologically and correct their spelling. This innovative approach combines two procedures commonly performed independently, as part of a structured approach called Structural Spelling Correction (SSC). The core advantage of SSC is its ability to address the intricate nature of the Arabic language, such as its complex writing system and extensive set of similar-looking letters. To achieve this, MADARi employs a unique method called the Spelling-Morphology Double-Path Algorithm, which involves two interconnected components: a morphological analyzer and a spell checker. The algorithm ensures accurate results by integrating the outputs from these two components, using a set of predefined rules to validate its findings against a comprehensive Arabic corpus. To facilitate user interaction, MADARi presents the markup and correction suggestions through an intuitive interface, where proposed modifications can be viewed alongside the underlying morphological structure of the input text. A notable feature of this tool is its ability to handle a range of user proficiency levels, from novice to expert, by offering a range of markup and correction options, including fully automated, semi-automated, and fully manual approaches. A notable aspect of MADARi is its ability to handle a range of user proficiency levels, from novice to expert, by incorporating a range of markup and correction options, including both automated and manual methods. Planetary systems surrounding G and K type stars offer ideal conditions to support life, which is often linked to the presence of a habitable zone where temperatures allow liquid water to exist. A key factor in assessing these planets' habitability is the photochemical impact on their atmospheric gases, which can be as significant as other factors like temperature and water levels. Overexpressed chemical products of these photochemical reactions may not only indicate a thin upper atmosphere but also suggest the breakdown of biomolecules, which could be detected from space. To address this, a new approach is developed which considers multiple gas species and their interactions to determine observable biomolecular signatures from an exoplanet's atmospheric gases. Applying this method to various types of stars and planetary environments, it is shown that the spectral analysis of an exoplanet is heavily dependent on the characteristics of its host star and planet. For example, planets surrounded by stars with higher levels of UV radiation result in the breakdown of certain organic molecules before they can reach Earth-like atmospheres. In contrast, planets that are close to their host stars or experience high levels of wind may not have sufficient UV protection, leading to the immediate destruction of biomolecules before they can leave the planet's atmosphere. Furthermore, it is also demonstrated that space-based telescopes such as HabEx and CHAI can detect gas species that are essential to life, such as oxygen, methane, and carbon dioxide, around planets that are similar in size and orbit to those of the TRAPPIST-

To address the challenge of identifying Majorana modes via tunneling spectroscopy, we are exploring an alternative approach that involves a different setup where the tunneling barrier is ohmic, and we have demonstrated the feasibility of this approach both theoretically and experimentally. The signature of an gapped Majorana mode is predicted to change in this setup from a zero-bias peak to a minimum at negative voltage values, thus providing a distinct hallmark for the mode's presence. Our research involves an ideal one-dimensional p-wave superconductor model that is both topologically non-trivial and proximitized, and we have established the theoretical foundation for our proposed technique. Furthermore, we have developed a new method for determining the normal state resistance of the probe, allowing us to distinguish the signature of a Majorana mode in tunneling spectroscopy, and this method is also applicable to other peaks.

The development of an intelligent road system, akin to those in other critical infrastructure categories like the power grid or transportation networks, relies heavily on advanced technologies like computer vision and machine learning. This paper outlines the design and functionality of a cutting-edge, all-encompassing system called RoadAtlas, which has been developed to streamline road defect detection, assessment, and maintenance through both real-world and simulated environments. By integrating specialized sensors, a robust software framework, and a user-friendly web interface, RoadAtlas facilitates real-time detection of road issues, including cracks, potholes, and lateral deviations, as well as temperature and vibration readings. Furthermore, this system enables data visualization, historical anomaly tracking, and customized alert systems for road maintenance teams.

The shadow bicategory is a new construction in framed bicategories, essentially making the part of the framed bicategory that's perpendicular to the base space reflect the properties of the base space. Our research shows that this concept is most accurately described by modifying the definition of a bicategorical bundle so that the base space and the bundle space are framed, and calling it a framed bicategorical bundle. This extension also allows us to define morphisms between framed bicategories. It turns out that the shadow bicategory is closely related to the concept of a bicategorical bundle having certain properties, and using this relationship we can prove that the homotopy category of the shadow bicategory is equivalent to the category of bundles over the base space. This result can be generalized to show that the homotopy category of a framed version of a given category is equivalent to the category of framed bundles over the base space with a given structure.

Research on robot auditory localization has been conducted for over two decades but precise sound localization remains elusive, with most methods falling short of human capability. This paper seeks to provide a comprehensive framework for the challenging task of sound localization, focusing on a simple auditory system and ignoring external distractions such as other sounds and the robot's own noise. A novel approach is presented, based on interaural time difference and sound pressure level, with a target error of 10 degrees. Twenty-four test sounds were selected, spanning a range of frequencies, covering all possible inner angles from 10 to 170 degrees in 10-degree increments, for a total of 240 test conditions. The results showed that the system can achieve highly accurate localization for certain frequencies but may stray from the target by as much as 40 degrees for other frequencies, indicating a significant role of frequency in the auditory localization process.
